articles.title: North Korea Expands Missiles and Drones With Russian Help
articles.body:
North Korea has advanced its ballistic missile systems and established mass production lines for strike drones with technical and operational assistance from Russia, The New York Times reported.
Moscow is transferring military technologies, telemetry feedback, and operational expertise to Pyongyang in exchange for North Korean ammunition, labor, and combat troops deployed in support of Russia’s war effort in Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In early October, North Korea conducted a test launch of a tactical ballistic missile that Pyongyang claimed is capable of delivering a nuclear warhead.
South Korean and Japanese defense tracking systems recorded the munition traveling approximately 700 kilometers (435 miles), whereas state media in Pyongyang asserted the missile achieved an operational flight range of 1,000 kilometers (621 miles).
Departing from routine diplomatic protocols that traditionally limit Seoul to brief statements of condemnation following Northern missile tests, South Korea conducted its first operational test of a domestically developed hypersonic ballistic missile five days later.
The test launch was observed in person by South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, reflecting growing institutional concern in Seoul regarding Pyongyang’s accelerated technological timeline.
Russian combat feedback, accuracy, and mass drone assembly
Western intelligence and defense analysts observe that Pyongyang is leveraging Russian operational data detailing how North Korean weapons perform in real combat environments against modern Western-supplied air defense systems.
Russian Drone Hits Vinnytsia Apartment Block, 6 Injured
Defense analyst Anton Ponomarenko noted that telemetry and performance feedback provided by the Russian military have enabled North Korean engineers to refine the guidance accuracy and terminal maneuverability of tactical ballistic missiles, increasing the conventional and nuclear strike risk posed to South Korea.
Concurrently, Moscow has assisted Pyongyang in establishing domestic industrial manufacturing lines for loitering munitions and strike drones.
Pyongyang has adapted lessons from the armed conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, where cost-effective unmanned platforms have repeatedly saturated and depleted advanced, high-cost air defense networks.
During North Korean military drills conducted last month, an integrated swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles conducted synchronized saturation strikes against an island target while cruise and ballistic missiles launched simultaneous strikes from multiple vectors.
Defense specialists emphasize that countering coordinated drone-swarm and missile saturation tactics could compel South Korea and its regional allies to overhaul integrated air and missile defense postures at substantial financial cost.
Expanding military alliance and troop deployments
The reciprocal technology transfers underscore the deepening military axis between Moscow and Pyongyang following the signing of a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Pyongyang in June 2024, which codified a mutual defense clause.
In a birthday dispatch addressed to Putin on Oct. 7, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un reaffirmed “invariable support” for Moscow, characterizing Russia’s war in Ukraine as a “sacred war of justice” and pledging to expand bilateral strategic alignment.
The partnership encompasses significant conventional transfers and frontline force commitments. North Korea has supplied artillery munitions and ballistic missiles to the Russian military while deploying an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 military personnel to Russian, including roughly 10,000 combat infantry and 1,000 military engineers deployed in the Kursk region.
According to casualty assessments compiled by South Korea’s National Intelligence Service (NIS), approximately 6,000 North Korean soldiers deployed in support of Russian operations have been killed or wounded in combat, reinforcing Pyongyang’s reliance on Russian technological reciprocity to compensate for troop and material losses.

articles.title: Saudi downs 10 Houthi missiles as Riyadh airport reopens
articles.body:
The New Arab's live blog is now closed. Here were the top stories:
Saudi Arabia has downed 10 Houthi ballistic missiles and a drone fired against the capital, Riyadh, according to the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised Yemeni government. Explosions were heard in Riyadh, according to AFP.
King Khalid International Airport has reopened terminals one and two following Houthi missile strikes in early October that killed 17 people and wounded over 330. Terminals three and four, which were struck by the Houthis, are yet to reopen.
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi is warning that any Israeli and US attack will not change the country's position, saying at an event in Tehran: "Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same."
The US embassy in Riyadh has announced that it has ordered non-emergency staffers and family members to leave Saudi Arabia, citing continued attacks by Yemen's Houthis against the country.
Security Alert: U.S. Mission Saudi Arabia (October 25, 2026) Effective October 23, 2026, the Department of State ordered non-emergency U.S. government employees and U.S. government employee family members to leave Saudi Arabia due to safety risks. Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions. The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area. U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization from Chief of Mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia following recent missile and UAV attacks on airports in the Kingdom. King Khalid International Airport (RUH) in Riyadh announced a partial reopening as of October 25 for domestic flights and some international flights operated by national carriers. A limited number of flights normally based at RUH are operating out of Qassim-based Prince Naif bin Abdulaziz International Airport (ELQ). Operations at King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah (JED) are operational with some delays and cancellations. Operations at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam (DMM) are operational with some delays and cancellations. U.S. citizens should be aware of potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations, and travel disruptions. Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia. We recommend checking your flight departure status directly with the airline and with the airport. Read more: https://t.co/Vgg95JTPsw
The commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM) has visited the Strait of Hormuz, saying a statement that the visit "underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
"Today, primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear of Iranian sea mines thanks to incredible efforts by our people," he said, adding that "we remain intensely focused on keeping commercial traffic flowing as we work with our teammates in the U.S. interagency, Gulf Cooperation Council, and shipping industry."
The visit comes amid tension between the US, Iran and Israel, as reports in US media continue to emerge of renewed preparations made by the US to strike Iran.
Sri Lanka coordinated the rescue of 40 Iranian sailors from multiple commercial ships in international waters off the coast of the country and supported their return to Iran, a spokesman for the island nation's foreign ministry said on Sunday.
The ministry received a request from the Iranian embassy via diplomatic channels to rescue the sailors, Thushara Rodrigo, a spokesman for the ministry, said, adding they had been suffering unspecified medical emergencies.
The ministry didn't give any further details of why they had to be rescued but local media including Indian national newspaper The Hindu reported they were on board vessels which were US-sanctioned oil tankers.
Washington has imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping as part of its war on Iran.
The sailors from 19 ships were brought ashore at Galle Harbour, about 126 km from commercial capital Colombo, and were given medical treatment before returning to Iran early on Sunday morning, the spokesman added.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections, warning the Islamic Republic against any hostile acts.
The premier has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, touting the war he launched against Iran in February alongside the United States and suggesting that he alone can see it through.
"We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," Netanyahu said in a video released by his office on Sunday.
"Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows," he added, noting the military was ready for both defensive and offensive operations.
Earlier in the day, the premier posted an AI-generated image of a mushroom cloud engulfing Tel Aviv, alongside text attributed to a right-wing political commentator calling Iran an existential threat and arguing that all the other issues discussed this election season were trivial in comparison.
The image was labelled as fearmongering by his opposition rivals.
The 2027 edition of the Dakar Rally has been moved out of Saudi Arabia due to security concerns, organisers Amaury Sport Organisation said on Sunday.
The event, due to take place in January and which has been held in Saudi Arabia since 2020, wouldmove to a different territory, with the location to be announced in the coming days, the ASO said in a statement.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that the Dakar Rally wouldtake place in Africa, citing sources involved in the World Rally-Raid Championship.
"Amaury Sport Organisation and Saudi Motorsport Company have jointly decided that Dakar Saudi Arabia 2027, scheduled from 1 to 15 January, 2027, will not be held in the Kingdom, following recent developments in the region," the ASO said.
Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday as part of an effort to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation told Reuters.
An Israeli strike on a university in Gaza City killed three people on Sunday, staff and a local hospital said, while the civil defence agency reported four others killed elsewhere in the territory.
Al Shifa hospital said it received three bodies and treated eight people who were wounded in the Gaza City drone strike, with two sources at the Islamic University saying those killed were administrative staff and the injured were students.
Gaza's education ministry said in a statement that the students had been present for classes.
It went on to condemn the strike and said "the global silence regarding attacks on students and universities serves as encouragement for the continuation of these crimes".
"This strike occurs at a time when the higher education sector is facing total annihilation, with 95 percent of the buildings belonging to academic institutions having been damaged as a result of the war," it continued.
"This heinous assault is part of a continuous series of attacks on education; over the past six days, 10 students and educators have been killed by the occupation's fire."
More than 100 economists, including former Bank of Israel officials, ex-central bank governor Jacob Frenkel and several Nobel laureates, signed a letter expressing alarm over Netanyahu's proposed crypto plan, saying it would lead to higher unemployment, a fall in foreign investment and the collapse of Israel's economic standing in the world.
In an interview with Israel's Channel 10 on Friday, Netanyahu said he was preparing for a scenario in which broader sanctions were imposed on Israel.
"There could be sanctions, and sanctions on banks so you need to set up a bypass economy," Netanyahu said. "You know, there are currencies that can bypass (sanctions). We are also working on that."
In response to Netanyahu's comments, the letter read: "As we have seen in countries that have suffered similar sanctions, such as South Africa, Iran, and Russia, the living standards of Israeli citizens would plummet dramatically, and the state's ability to finance its security and defend itself against its enemies would be severely damaged."
"Netanyahu is knowingly leading the State of Israel toward boycott and international economic isolation, and all he has to offer the Israeli economy is a puzzling solution, one accepted in criminal organisations, that will not help in the slightest."
Israeli forces have demolished Palestinian homes and businesses in Hebron and forcibly displaced around 2,500 people, according to Palestinian rights monitors, as a sweeping military crackdown entered its third day on Sunday with further raids and arrests across the southern occupied West Bank.
Bulldozers have torn through residential and commercial areas, with footage showing homes reduced to rubble across several blocks. The demolitions follow Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's threat to destroy the neighbourhood from which two Palestinian gunmen allegedly came after an attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday.
The Palestinian Centre for Human Rights (PCHR), citing preliminary estimates from Hebron municipality, said approximately 500 families comprising around 2,500 people had been forced from their homes in an area spanning 350 dunums, or 35 hectares. Israeli forces have sealed the area and continued house searches, leaving displaced residents uncertain when they will be allowed to return.
The operation has targeted Ein Deir Baha and surrounding neighbourhoods, alongside homes, businesses and industrial facilities in Farsh al-Hawa.
PCHR documented the demolition of a three-storey house, a commercial facility selling car parts and the walls surrounding a tile and ceramics business's yard. The organisation said the house was demolished despite its owner having obtained an interim court order following an earlier demolition notice.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has published a photo of a nuclear strike on Tel Aviv as a warning in the event he is not reelected as PM, a move opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot described as 'fearmongering'
In the post made on X, Netanyahu says that "if the Iranians obtain nuclear weapons, nothing else will matter anymore," including the controversies around his premiership, such as allowing the evasion of the Ultra-Orthodox draft, adding that Israeli voters should vote for a candidate that can "complete the mission" or expose the country to a "second holocaust."
Netanyahu also went on to warn that finishing the job against Iran would not happen by a candidate that requires the support of "Muslim Brotherhood and terror enablers", a reference to Israel's Palestinian parties that could be well placed to determine the next government, as both Netanyahu and Opposition blocs poll under the 61-seat threshold to form a government.
Palestinian parties have consistently been used as a scare tactic in the election to warn against votes for Eisenkot's coalition.
Eisenkot responded by calling Netanyahu "hysterical", adding that "as in every election campaign, it's the same method of lies and scare tactics. This time, threatening Israeli citizens with mass destruction. And this is after you failed to achieve the objectives of the war in Iran."
Democrats head Yair Golan, part of Eisenkot's bloc, also responded, saying: "On Tuesday, we will replace those who sow panic and restore security and sanity to Israel."
Saudi Arabia issued danger warnings, which have since passed, for the Jazan and Taif regions of the country, as Yemen's Houthis continue to launch ballistic missiles and drones against the country.
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10 percent, with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches.
While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by war with the United States and Israel that began in February.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the two countries struck key Iranian infrastructure, including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
Winter in Iran often sees temperatures drop below freezing, especially in the country's north.
"To get through the approaching winter, a nationwide effort is essential ... to reduce gas consumption by at least 10 percent," said Ghalibaf in a video carried by Iranian media.
"Anyone who saves gas, regardless of the amount, will immediately receive the corresponding proceeds in their bank account, allowing everyone to see the tangible impact of those savings on their household budget."
Tehran strikes Iranian Kurdish base in Iraq with drones
Iran's armed forces attacked bases belonging to an Iranian Kurdish opposition group in Iraq's Kurdistan region using drones, a media outlet in Tehran reported on Sunday.
"As part of a drone operation carried out by the Revolutionary Guards' ground forces, the headquarters of the terrorist and separatist group Komala, located in the Balisan region, was targeted last night," the Mehr news agency said.
The semi-autonomous region hosts camps and bases belonging to several groups of Iranian Kurdish militants, which Iran has targeted repeatedly since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
The Revolutionary Guards have not immediately claimed responsibility for the strikes on these fighters, whom Iran accuses of being supported by Israel, its sworn enemy.
In the most deadly recent attack, nine Komala members were killed on 17 July near the city of Sulaymaniyah.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition announced that it has intercepted 10 ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia's southern region.

Iran’s air defence systems shot down a US LUCAS drone over the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, the Iranian army said on Sunday, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's position.
The remarks come amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on 28 February.
"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."
An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

articles.title: ‘Trump Is Cooked’: Republicans Clash Over Ukraine as Midterms Loom
articles.body:
“I think Trump is cooked in the midterms, unless literally every poll is disgustingly wrong.”
This assessment came from a Republican-adjacent Washington source speaking to Kyiv Post on condition of anonymity as US President Donald Trump’s handling of Russia’s war against Ukraine draws unusually public criticism from his own party.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I don’t think [Trump’s] efforts to scapegoat Ukraine will make that worse, but he’s also not getting away with it,” the source added. The latest sentiment comes on the heels of Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff traveling to St. Petersburg to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin for a new round of negotiations, during which he referred to Putin as a “humanitarian”. Meanwhile, Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian cities and Kyiv reported restricted access to satellite communications essential to frontline operations and intercepting Russian drones.
For Republican commentators and politicians who had spent months pushing the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, this was an unpleasant sight. They found themselves watching the US offer Russia economic relief while pressing Ukraine for concessions and restricting its defense capabilities.
Beyond immediate moral discomfort and questions on Washington’s foreign policy priorities, there’s also the practical aspect as they seek re-election during the Nov. 3 midterms. With all 435 House seats and roughly a third of the Senate contested, the Republican party’s chances of preserving a majority in both chambers risks slipping away as Trump’s approval rating continues to plunge.
Missiles Strike Energiya Defense Battery Plant in Yelets
The undone MAGA momentum
In late July, conservative MAGA commentator Laura Loomer made headlines. Formerly a fierce critic of Ukraine, she traveled to Kyiv to interview President Volodymyr Zelensky, publicly acknowledging that she had repeated Russian propaganda before realizing Moscow’s support for Iran in its confrontation with Israel and the US – a circumstance that helped change her position.
This is how she became part of an emerging pro-Ukraine conservative camp alongside figures such as Ben Shapiro, who had also interviewed Zelensky, as well as Mark Levin and other prominent Trump-adjacent commentators.
For a country often presented to some Republican audiences as a burden on American taxpayers, this was a significant opening and a promising one as well, since the renewed enthusiasm reinforced the case for the sanctions championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. The logic was that if Russia would not agree to a ceasefire or a negotiated end to the war, it should face a heavier economic cost for continuing the invasion.
The momentum bore fruit: Congress passed the bill, and Trump signed it into law on Sept. 18. Key provisions were due to take effect by Oct. 18, although the legislation also gave the president broad waiver powers.
Yet what appeared to be a breakthrough soon became a full-fledged retreat.
Instead of imposing those additional penalties, Trump abruptly announced his diesel agreement with Moscow on Oct. 9.
A week later, he waived major new sanctions and duties under the Graham legislation (though leaving existing sanctions in place) and launched what Susan B. Glasser of The New Yorker coined as a pre-election campaign against Zelensky, toward whom his antipathy is long documented.
Trump blamed Ukraine’s refinery attacks for aggravating fuel shortages and suggested that a settlement would require different Ukrainian leadership, while thanking Putin for presumably being “the reasonable one” in the illegal war he started.
This time, however, the pressure went beyond personal attacks: intelligence sharing, satellite access and weapons deliveries had become part of the dispute, accompanied by a considerably more Moscow-friendly rhetoric than in spring when the US resorted to similar ways of pressuring the victim of Russia’s aggression.
Republicans push back
Glasser’s description of Trump’s actions might be easy for his supporters to dismiss as criticism from a familiar opponent. The reaction from Republicans themselves, however, was harder to explain away with freshly-converted Loomer saying: “Buying Russian oil puts money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran that chants Death to America. We know this.”
While disagreements with Zelensky, including concerns about corruption and oversight, were not unusual for many Republicans, restricting Ukraine’s ability to defend itself while offering economic relief to Russia was another.
“What is interesting is that his recent, unveiled support for Putin has finally seen some anger from Congressional Republicans,” the source told Kyiv Post, warning that some of them “are leaving office.”
Reacting to Witkoff’s salute to Putin in St. Petersburg as a “humanitarian” for releasing American detainee Stephen Hubbard, another Republican-adjacent source privately told Kyiv Post: “I so hate Witkoff.”
The anger, however, was not limited to private conversations. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis responded in very strong terms to Witkoff’s flattery, asking:: “WTF, Steve?” Separately, Sen. John Cornyn described Putin as a “stone cold killer.”
Hours after the meeting, Russia launched another attack on Kyiv.
The backlash followed strong objections to the privately-struck diesel deal. Tillis, Susan Collins and Mitch McConnell joined a bipartisan letter urging Trump to reverse the agreement, arguing that it would offer limited relief to American consumers while supplying revenue to Moscow.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, standing for reelection in Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District pursued legislation to block Russian energy purchases. European governments also rejected following Washington’s lead on sanctions relief.
Then came the reports of restrictions on intelligence and satellite communications that only served to intensify the tensions on Capitol Hill.
Zelensky said on Oct. 20 that US intelligence sharing had resumed. Satellite access took longer to improve: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starlink and defense-tailored Starshield services had disrupted connections on fast-moving equipment, including Ukrainian drones.
On Oct. 24, Ukrainian defense specialists reported that terminals were operating above the previous 161 km/h limit. Later that morning, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara reported stable connections above 400 km/h.
But Patriot interceptor deliveries remained delayed, according to Zelensky’s remarks reported that day. Restored intelligence and communications did not resolve the shortage of missiles needed to intercept Russian attacks.
For Republicans seeking re-election, these developments leave an awkward question to answer: what has Washington attained by this and how it does affect them?
Trump vs. American voters
Despite the existing notion among some that the Republicans are Russia-friendly, the evidence paints a different picture.
Earlier Pew polling found that 47% of Republicans regarded Russia as an enemy. Across Americans, 83% viewed Russia unfavorably.
The real partisan Ukraine disagreement lies in two distinct domains: US budgetary and culture wars. The former comes down to the idea of spending and how it affects the average person’s ability to fulfill the basic American idea of buying a home, which, unlike today, used to be a largely affordable endeavor.
The latter is more poignantly about which way American society should be heading: toward a more secular group with the progressive agenda dominating the mainstream view, or the opposite.
Ukraine got trapped in both as it needs money from an already heavily indebted society and the idea, often spread by Russian propagandists and other malign agents, that it’s a Democratic stronghold of progressive thought.
Both affect the Republican stance toward Kyiv, even if they view Ukraine’s resistance as a legitimate fight at large, which is reflected in the Republican polling ahead of the looming midterms.
University of Maryland surveys, conducted between July 21 and Aug. 17, found Republican majorities supporting continued military assistance to Ukraine in 31 of 39 battleground states and congressional districts surveyed.
The question covered equipment, ammunition, training and intelligence — including capabilities subsequently drawn into October’s disputes.
To understand what that means practically for Republicans, beyond the question of why deal with Putin in the first place, requires consideration of what House members must do when they return to their districts: explain not only why they supported or opposed a particular bill, but also the direction of their party’s policies.
The risk? A backlash.
This is what happened to Ukraine-born Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz who encountered an angry crowd at a March 2025 town hall in Indiana, where questions about Ukraine accompanied criticism of federal spending cuts and other Trump policies.
Republican lawmakers thus face a two-sided task. On the one hand, attacking their party’s leader risks alienating his supporters. On the other hand, defending him without qualification means explaining policies that some of their own constituents oppose – including what Kyiv Post’s source described as “unveiled support for Putin.”
Nor can they simply rely on the “Trump effect,” hoping his endorsement will improve their prospects: A New York Times/Siena survey released on Oct. 21 put Trump’s approval at 36%, against 59% disapproval. Approval of his handling of the cost of living stood at 29%; on gas prices, it was 24%.
Even if candidates can persuade their core supporters that the diesel deal, admittedly, supported by over 50% of the Republican voters, was necessary, winning a competitive election requires more than securing the loyalty of the core base.
The independents the Republicans need
In majoritarian systems, which operate on the “winner takes it all” principle, candidates also need voters who are not reliably behind their party. That includes swing voters and independents, although the two groups are not interchangeable.
Here is where Republicans face less encouraging news.
Independents opposed the diesel deal by 71% to 10%, while opposition among all respondents stood at 63%.
“The diesel fuel deal does almost nothing to help diesel prices, but it does damage Republicans politically. Trump needs Independents to vote Republican,” Steven Moore recently wrote.
Moore is a former Republican congressional chief of staff and founder of the Ukraine Freedom Project, which has worked to build conservative support for Kyiv.
Depending on how much weight these voters give foreign policy, their dissatisfaction could help Democratic candidates or weaken Republican turnout. The survey does not measure whether the deal will change their votes, but the gap between Republican and independent opinion is substantial and cannot be ignored.
They could still vote Republican for other reasons, from economic policy to cultural issues.
Or, they could opt for a Democrat if they choose to show at the polling stations at all, given that fewer than half of eligible Americans voted in recent midterms.
What if the Democrats win?
If there’s anything to learn from Trump’s handling of electoral defeats, it’s that he strongly rules out such possibilities per se. This is why the recent actions aimed at preparing to contest the outcome if they’re not favorable to the Republican Party should be taken into consideration – even if they do not result in substantial practical and societal repercussions.
Yet any hope in Kyiv, or in some European capitals, that a Democratic victory would automatically restore generous and predictable funding, would be misplaced.
Ukraine appears to have a difficult time navigating the American political landscape and how to approach it – an impression stemming from Zelensky’s former right-hand man Andriy Yermak’s confession that he does not wish to understand Washington’s political ins and outs. He’s resigned due to alleged involvement in a large-scale corruption scandal.
The former US Ambassador Oksana Markarova’s perceived Democratic sympathies coupled with the corruption allegations involving her recently-resigned successor Olha Stefanishyna and today’s absence of a newly-appointed ambassador further complicate Kyiv’s positions on Capitol Hill, which bears little resemblance to its 2022 version when both the Democrats and the Republicans voted in favor of providing aid to Ukraine.
What would change more immediately if the Democrats take over is the political pressure on the administration.
If Democrats take the House, they would be positioned to replace Mike Johnson as speaker, control committees and pursue investigations. Ukraine would almost certainly feature in that confrontation, as Kyiv Post’s source predicts: “Democrats with both houses will be launching a salvo of investigations and even impeachment hearings. Trump’s nonsense toward Ukraine will definitely be part of that.”
In fact, the scrutiny of the administration’s decisions is already underway.
On Oct. 22, Sen. Richard Blumenthal announced an inquiry into restrictions on Starlink and Starshield, seeking information from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Musk about who authorized the changes and how they were implemented.
The inquiry also examines the Pentagon’s dependence on SpaceX and whether US forces could face similar disruptions. Restoring Ukraine’s access does not settle who restricted it or why.
A Democratic House would give those investigations greater institutional backing, including control over hearing agendas and the pursuit of documents and testimony. The sanctions waivers and diesel agreement would offer further subjects for scrutiny.
But scrutiny and the reversal of current aid-absent policy aren’t identical endeavors.
Some Democrats, like Ilhan Omar voted against Graham’s sanctions, and even if Democrats initiate another Ukraine aid package, or if Fitzpatrick-initiate bipartisan Ukraine Support Act, which passed the House on June 4 and proposed additional assistance for Kyiv alongside sanctions against Russia, appears on the Senate floor with enough “yays,” it would still need Trump’s signature.
Little suggests that the man who thanks Putin, has his envoy call him a humanitarian, and floats 200% tariffs on both Ukraine and Russia to force them into a peace deal, will do just that.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian titanium plant more than 1,400 kilometers from border, monitoring channel claims
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes Russian titanium plant, facility producing missile, drone components, monitoring channels claim
Editor's note: This story was updated to include details of a reported Ukrainian attack on Lipetsk Oblast.
Ukrainian forces struck Avisma, one of the world's largest titanium sponge producers in Russia's Perm Krai, and the Energiya plant in Lipetsk Oblast, which manufactures components for missile systems and drones, on Oct. 25, Ukrainian and Russian monitoring channels reported.
Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin said at around 11 a.m. local time that 11 drones had been downed during a Ukrainian attack on the region.
Makhonin added that an "industrial facility" in the northern part of the region had sustained "minor" damage but continued to operate as normal. The governor did not specify which facility had been damaged.
According to Makhonin, five employees of the facility were also injured in the Ukrainian attack.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said the strike targeted Avisma in the town of Berezniki, located about 170 kilometers (105 miles) from the regional center of Perm. The plant is part of Russian metallurgical corporation VSMPO-AVISMA.
Located more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles) from the Ukrainian-Russian border, Avisma has been under U.S. sanctions since 2023. The plant manufactures products used in military aircraft, nuclear submarines, armored vehicles, and missile systems.
Later in the day, Ukrainian forces also attacked the Energiya plant in the city of Yelets, in Russia's Lipetsk Oblast, more than 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the Russian independent media outlet Astra reported, citing open-source intelligence (OSINT) data.
Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov said an "industrial zone" had been targeted, injuring one person. The governor did not identify the facility that came under attack.
Energiya is Russia's largest research and production enterprise specializing in electrochemical power sources. Its products are used across various sectors, including the defense industry, civil aviation, maritime transport and energy. The plant manufactures batteries for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), power sources for air defense missile systems, and batteries for aircraft and naval vessels.
The enterprise is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the European Union, the U.K., Canada, Switzerland, Japan, Australia and Ukraine.
The plant was previously attacked in May and July 2025, as well as in January 2026.
Ukraine had not commented on the reported strikes in Lipetsk Oblast and Perm Krai at the time of publication.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Ukraine's General Staff said Ukrainian forces also struck Russian military radar stations in Belgorod Oblast overnight on Oct. 25, as well as a Russian command post in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast and a command-and-observation post in occupied Kherson Oblast.
Other targets included concentrations of Russian troops in the occupied parts of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, the General Staff added.
Earlier, Ukrainian monitoring channels reported a fire at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk following a Ukrainian attack.
The overnight attack on Belgorod also damaged a local shopping and entertainment center, monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported.
Belgorod Mayor Valentin Demidov said one person was killed and 10 others were injured in the attack. Residential buildings and cars were also damaged, he added.

articles.title: Strikes on oil refineries and dozens of Russian vessels: how the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ secret unit operates
articles.body:
Strikes on oil refineries and dozens of Russian vessels: how the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ secret unit operates
Kyiv • UNN
The Kairos unit was transformed into the 7th Separate Center with hundreds of military personnel. It coordinates long-range strikes on Russian targets.
The Ukrainian Kairos battalion, which participates in long-range strikes against Russian facilities, has been deployed within the 7th Separate Center of the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces. This was reported by Bloomberg, according to UNN.
Details
According to the agency, the Kairos unit, which was previously part of the 414th Separate Brigade of Unmanned Systems “Magyar’s Birds,” has evolved into a much larger military structure. The 7th Separate Center now numbers hundreds of service members and is capable of coordinating operations by other units.
The commander of the formation, known by the call sign “Ray,” told journalists that the capabilities of Ukraine’s long-range strikes have grown significantly. Whereas previously drones could carry out missions at a distance of about 100 kilometers and carry a relatively small warhead, Ukrainian forces now use significantly more powerful weapons, including relatively inexpensive cruise missiles.
One of Kairos’s areas of activity has been attacks on Russian maritime logistics. According to the commander, over the course of one month the unit struck 60 vessels in the Sea of Azov. In addition, during the summer campaign aimed at isolating occupied Crimea, the Unmanned Systems Forces carried out approximately 7,000 strikes using drones. These figures were provided by the Ukrainian side; there has been no independent confirmation of all the claimed results.
Bloomberg also reports on Kairos’s involvement in large-scale attacks on Russian energy facilities. In particular, the unit took part in an operation to attack the territory of the Moscow oil refinery in Kapotnya on September 20, 2026. Following the attack, the facility suspended oil refining, and repairs to the damaged equipment could take several weeks.
Satellite reconnaissance and data analysis play an important role in preparing long-range strikes. Ukrainian forces use current and archival satellite imagery to study Russian facilities. Specialists with experience in the energy sector are also involved in planning the operations.
According to the agency’s assessment, the expansion of the capabilities of Ukrainian long-range strike units demonstrates significant changes in the conduct of the war. Ukraine is increasingly using its own technologies, intelligence data, and coordinated operations to strike Russia’s military and energy infrastructure at a considerable distance from the front line.
We remind you
Earlier, the British publication The Times reported on the activities of the Ukrainian Kairos unit, which takes part in strikes against facilities on Russian territory. Subsequently, Reuters and The Guardian published reports on Ukrainian military operations against Russian maritime logistics and military infrastructure in the occupied territories.

articles.title: The Arctic giant: How Russia dominates the frozen frontier
articles.body:
The Arctic giant: What the West won’t tell you about Russia’s northern frontier
“Russia’s future... lies in the Arctic,” President Vladimir Putin declared last year, portraying the frozen north as a cornerstone of national prosperity for generations to come.
One look at a map shows why: The country accounts for approximately 53% of the Arctic Ocean’s coastline, according to the Arctic Council, making it the world’s largest Arctic power in geographical terms.
However, the stakes go well beyond geography, as Russia’s Arctic territories contain enormous oil, gas, and mineral reserves, host vital elements of its nuclear deterrent, and accommodate multiple military bases.
As climate change and retreating sea ice gradually open new opportunities for maritime navigation, Moscow is also seeking to transform the Northern Sea Route into a lucrative trade artery connecting Europe and Asia.
Meanwhile, both NATO and the EU are increasingly challenging Russia’s traditional presence in the Arctic. On October 20, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the region as the “frontline of global power competition,” accusing Moscow of militarization while setting course on expanding cooperation with NATO, developing military logistics corridors, and catching up with Moscow in its icebreaker capacity.
Russia maintains that it has “never threatened anyone in the Arctic” but vowed to safeguard its sovereign interests while accusing NATO of escalating tensions.
But what exactly makes the Russian Arctic so special, and why is Moscow so determined to stand its ground there?
What defines the Arctic?
Unlike Antarctica, which is a continent surrounded by ocean, the Arctic is an ocean surrounded by the northern reaches of Eurasia and North America, Greenland, and numerous islands. The region’s generally accepted geographical boundary is the Arctic Circle, beyond which the sun can remain above the horizon for 24 hours during summer and disappear entirely for at least one day during winter.
Eight countries have territories in the Arctic: Russia, Canada, the United States, Denmark through Greenland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Iceland, with the first five having coastlines directly bordering the Arctic Ocean – which gives them an important role in determining maritime boundaries and access to resources.
The region is characterized by extreme cold, extensive sea ice, permafrost, prolonged polar darkness during winter, and continuous daylight during summer. Temperatures can fall below -40C in continental areas, while thick sea ice, storms, and limited infrastructure make transportation and industrial operations exceptionally challenging.
However, the Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average, creating unprecedented opportunities for maritime trade and resource exploitation, even if thawing permafrost threatens existing infrastructure.
Who owns what in the Arctic?
Russia, Canada, the US, Denmark, and Norway – countries bordering the Arctic Ocean – exercise sovereignty over their established land territories and islands, as well as their territorial waters extending up to 12 nautical miles offshore. Coastal states also enjoy exclusive rights to natural resources within a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone.
However, their rights can extend considerably farther if they establish that the seabed beyond this limit forms part of their continental shelf. This is where high-stakes game begins, as countries with rights over an extended continental shelf can exclusively explore and exploit its oil, gas, and mineral resources.
The Arctic is estimated to hold 90 billion barrels of oil and 1,669 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in undiscovered and recoverable reserves alone, on top of abundant deposits of nickel, copper, palladium, iron ore, zinc, lead, phosphate, and bauxite. To put it into perspective, OPEC estimates Russia’s entire proven reserves at 80 billion barrels of crude oil and approximately 1,483 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.
At the same time, extended continental shelf rights are not equal to territorial sovereignty, with the waters remaining open to international navigation.
Russia was the first country to formally seek recognition of an extended Arctic continental shelf, submitting several claims to a UN commission since 2001. The commission requested additional scientific evidence, prompting Moscow to conduct extensive Arctic expeditions.
Other countries joined the Arctic race: Denmark submitted claims in 2014, followed by Canada in 2019. After Russia significantly expanded its proposed continental shelf in 2021, Canada responded with an enlarged claim in 2022, complaining that Moscow’s move had tripled the area overlapping with its own submission.
However, Moscow has made significant strides in defending its claims. In 2023, the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf largely endorsed Russia’s geological arguments, supporting an extended shelf encompassing an estimated 1.8 million sq km.
Yet UN recommendations alone do not settle the dispute. Russia, Canada, and Denmark must still resolve their overlapping entitlements through negotiations or other lawful means. The outcome is not entirely without precedent, as Russia and Norway managed to settle a decades-long disagreement over approximately 175,000 sq km of the Barents Sea in 2010.
What does the Russian Arctic look like?
Russia’s Arctic stretches from the Kola Peninsula near Norway in the west to Chukotka opposite Alaska in the east, with the total coastline spanning more than 24,000 km. Russia’s officially designated Arctic Zone covers approximately 4.8 million sq km, or 28% of the country’s territory, and encompasses entire administrative regions, from Murmansk in the west to northern Yakutia in the east.
The landscape varies from rocky coastlines and tundra plains to frozen wetlands and vast taiga forests. Farther north lie remote archipelagos, including Novaya Zemlya, Franz Josef Land, Severnaya Zemlya, and the New Siberian Islands, some of which are extensively covered by glaciers and permanent ice. Novaya Zemlya also served as a major Soviet nuclear weapons testing ground.
The Russian Arctic is home to nearly 2.5 million people, with the region generating an estimated 7% of national GDP and 11% of its exports as of 2025.
Despite its unforgiving climate, the Russian Arctic is far from an empty wilderness. Its major population and industrial centers include Murmansk – the world’s largest city north of the Arctic Circle with a population of 260,000 which is also a major ice-free port – and Norilsk, a powerhouse of nickel, copper, and palladium production.
Other important Arctic Zone centers include Arkhangelsk and Severodvinsk, known for maritime industries and nuclear submarine construction, as well as Vorkuta, Salekhard, and the gas-producing hub of Novy Urengoy.
Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District is also the site of Novatek’s Yamal LNG plant, the largest of its kind in Russia, which exports gas through the port of Sabetta. Farther east, Pevek is home to the Akademik Lomonosov, the world’s only floating nuclear power plant.
The unique design is dictated by necessity: Western Chukotka is cut off from Russia’s national power grid, while the NPP was built at a shipyard and transported to the remote location by sea, avoiding major problems associated with construction of an ordinary nuclear facility.
How important is the Arctic to Russia, and vice versa?
Russia’s Arctic Zone is an economic powerhouse, underpinning its energy exports and supplying critical raw materials, hosting more than 80% of national natural gas production, alongside substantial shares of its oil, nickel, and platinum-group metal output. Major industrial complexes, including the Yamal gas fields and Norilsk mining operations, are central not only to Russia’s welfare, but also to global energy and commodity markets.
As for trade, Russia’s ports, major Siberian rivers, and icebreaker fleet – the largest in the world – form an extensive transportation network connecting resource-rich territories with international markets.
In this vein, the Northern Sea Route is now emerging as the most important Arctic itinerary due to climate change, having handled more than 37 million tons of cargo in 2025, including 5.4 million tons transported between Russian and Chinese ports.
Despite tensions with the West over the Ukraine conflict, Russia continues to participate in limited Arctic Council cooperation, including technical work on environmental monitoring and other shared regional challenges.
Why is the Arctic a key military stronghold for Russia?
Beyond its economic importance, the Arctic is a cornerstone of Russia’s national security, hosting crucial elements of its nuclear deterrent and providing strategic access to the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
The Kola Peninsula, bordering Norway and Finland, anchors the Northern Fleet and its nuclear-armed submarines, while an extensive network of airfields, radar installations, missile defenses, and military bases protects Russia’s northern approaches. Since the early 2010s, Moscow has also been restoring numerous Soviet-era facilities across remote Arctic islands.
The importance of the Arctic only increased after Finland and Sweden acceded to NATO in 2023 and 2024, respectively, leaving Russia as the only non-NATO member among the eight Arctic states.
Moscow subsequently sounded the alarm about the bloc’s expanding presence near its strategic naval bases. This year, NATO launched the so-called Arctic Sentry initiative, aimed at strengthening military coordination and surveillance, with joint drills involving tens of thousands of troops.
The EU, meanwhile, is also looking to interfere in regional affairs, with the bloc’s new Arctic Strategy envisaging the development of military logistics, upgrading ports and airports for military use, expanding icebreaker fleets, and increasing satellite surveillance of the region and tracking of Russian oil tankers.
In light of Western countries’ saber-rattling, Putin accused NATO of increasingly treating the Far North as a “springboard for potential conflicts,” warning that “we will proceed from current realities and will respond to all this.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov went further, accusing NATO of deliberately militarizing the Arctic, stressing that “such military activity in the Far North poses a direct threat to Russia’s security.” He also warned that escalating tensions could trigger an armed clash with “potentially disastrous consequences.”
How powerful is Russia’s icebreaker fleet?
Russia’s icebreaker fleet is in a league of its own, comparable in numbers to the rest of the world combined. The country operates 43 icebreakers, including eight nuclear-powered vessels and 35 diesel-electric ships.
Nuclear icebreakers are particularly formidable as they can operate for extended periods without refueling, maintaining access to remote ports, and escorting commercial ships through heavily ice-covered waters. Russia’s four modern 60-megawatt Project 22220 icebreakers are designed to break through ice up to approximately 2.8 meters thick.
Moscow also continues to press its icebreaker advantage, with plans to commission four additional nuclear icebreakers that are now at various stages of development. These include the behemoth Project 10510 Rossiya, designed to deliver 120 megawatts of propulsion power and support navigation through even thicker Arctic ice. The icebreaker is expected to be ready for operations in late 2029.
Russia’s icebreaker fleet is far ahead of the American one, which only operates three polar icebreakers – a shortcoming several US administrations described as a national security concern.
As for the EU, it collectively operates around ten icebreakers, depending on classification. The bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, acknowledged the gap, declaring that “in the Arctic, icebreakers are the measure of power,” with plans to explore joint procurement, though these efforts are unlikely to yield results for many years.
How does Russia govern the Arctic?
Given the region’s undeniable importance, Moscow has built an extensive state apparatus dedicated to managing its northern territories.While overall priorities and strategic vision are set by Putin personally, much of the federal coordination falls to Deputy Prime Minister Yury Trutnev, who chairs the State Commission for Arctic Development. Established in 2015, the body brings together senior officials, regional governors and representatives of major companies to coordinate economic, infrastructure and security policies.
The region is also overseen by the designated Ministry for the Development of the Russian Far East and Arctic, headed by Aleksey Chekunkov, which handles Arctic development policy, investment incentives, and socioeconomic programs.
As for the Arctic’s maritime portfolio, it is supervised by former Russian Security Council Secretary Nikolay Patrushev, now a presidential aide, who chairs the Maritime Board, established in 2024 to coordinate maritime strategy and defend Russia’s interests at sea.
Russia’s state nuclear corporation, Rosatom, also plays a significant role in the region while managing the Northern Sea Route infrastructure and nuclear icebreaker fleet. Murmansk Governor Andrey Chibis also chairs a dedicated State Council commission on the Northern Sea Route and the Arctic, helping coordinate regional development proposals.
The Russian government has also for years run several incentivizing special programs in the region, including a preferential business regime offering qualifying companies multi-year tax breaks and reduced social insurance contributions.
Moscow also operates the Arctic Hectare program, allowing eligible citizens to obtain up to one hectare of land for development completely free of charge, with the possibility of subsequently obtaining ownership, and the Arctic Mortgage scheme, offering qualifying borrowers subsidized housing loans at rates of up to 2%.
Some of the Arctic Zone regions boast the highest average salaries nationally. According to Rosstat, average gross monthly salaries in 2025 reached approximately 215,000 rubles ($2,570) in Chukotka and 178,000 rubles ($2,130) in the Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Area – a level exceeding or comparable to Moscow’s and higher than the national average of 100,000 rubles ($1,200). However, the financial advantages are partly offset by higher living costs.
The region also benefits from a dedicated Soviet-inherited Northern Delivery system that coordinates supplies of essential goods to remote settlements.
How did Russia develop its Arctic frontier?
While indigenous peoples inhabited the region for thousands of years, Russian Pomor seafarers first began exploring the White and Barents Seas in the Middle Ages, establishing trading and fishing settlements. However, a full-scale expansion picked up steam only in the 16th century and beyond.
The most dramatic transformation took place in the Soviet era, when Moscow poured major resources into polar exploration, industrialization, and transportation infrastructure. In 1932, the Soviet icebreaking steamer Alexander Sibiryakov became the first vessel to traverse the Northern Sea Route in a single navigation season.
Another landmark achievement came in 1959 when the Soviet Union commissioned the Lenin, the world’s first nuclear-powered icebreaker, allowing ships to operate in the Arctic for extended periods of time. During the Cold War, Moscow also heavily invested in naval and submarine bases in the region.
Following the Soviet collapse in 1991, investment plunged, infrastructure deteriorated, and northern shipping declined. However, Russia began rebuilding its Arctic presence in the 2000s, developing major energy projects, reviving military facilities, and expanding its icebreaker capabilities.
How is Russia investing in the Arctic?
Moscow has made Arctic development a long-term national priority, with the current strategy running through 2035. According to Russian officials, more than 1,000 state-supported projects have been launched in the region since 2020, attracting approximately 2.6 trillion rubles ($32 billion) in investment. Moscow expects total investment over the coming decade to exceed 30 trillion rubles.
Much of the effort is focused on natural resources, as major companies, including Gazprom, Rosneft, Novatek, and Nornickel, are expanding oil, gas, and mining operations, while the government offers preferential tax arrangements and other incentives to attract investors.
Moscow is also modernizing Arctic ports, expanding railway connections, and developing specialized cargo fleets. Apart from building icebreakers, it plans to construct at least ten rescue vessels and launch 12 weather-monitoring and radar satellites by 2035 in a bid to support more reliable navigation along the Northern Sea Route.
The military development remains another priority, with Russia continuing to modernize airfields and bases, strengthening the Northern Fleet and expanding the number of personnel deployed in the region. Last year, Putin also ordered the extension of a military-town renovation program through at least 2030, with a minimum of 10 billion rubles in annual federal funding.
Bottom Line
While the Arctic race has been overshadowed by the Russia-West standoff over Ukraine, the region remains crucial to Russia’s long-term interests. The Arctic’s enormous natural reserves underpin the national economy, and its military bases form an indispensable part of Russia’s nuclear deterrent, while the Northern Sea Route promises lucrative trade opportunities along the country’s vast northern coastline.
As both NATO and the EU hanker after influence in the region, Russia has made clear that it has no intention of surrendering its longstanding position. For the Arctic giant, the frozen frontier is far more than a distant outpost or a peripheral prize – it is a cornerstone of its security, prosperity, and future.

articles.title: Drones Strike Russian Titanium Producer Avisma in Urals
articles.body:
Long-range strike drones struck the “Avisma” titanium and chemical-metallurgical plant in the city of Berezniki in Russia’s Perm region overnight into Sunday, Oct. 25, targeting one of the world’s largest titanium production facilities, The Moscow Times and independent monitoring groups reported.
The enterprise operates as a subsidiary production division of VSMPO-Avisma Corporation, the world’s leading manufacturer of titanium sponge, specialized titanium alloys, and raw magnesium.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Perm Region Governor Dmitry Makhonin acknowledged the aerial incursion on Sunday, stating that an industrial enterprise situated in the northern sector of the province sustained “minor damage” following an attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
Makhonin claimed that the damaged facility continues to operate under standard routines and reported no casualties.
However, Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the drone strikes engaged the production grounds of the Avisma chemical-metallurgical facility in Berezniki.
Local residents similarly reported hearing multiple drone engines followed by detonations and the sound of air defense engagements in the vicinity of the plant’s industrial perimeter.
Strategic defense metallurgy and aerospace components
The Berezniki metallurgical complex functions as an irreplaceable industrial node within the Russian Federation’s defense-industrial supply chain.
Trump Eyes Post-War Business Ties With Both Ukraine and Russia
Avisma specializes in the chemical processing of ilmenite ore into titanium tetrachloride and the subsequent thermal reduction of titanium sponge, alongside refining metallic magnesium and magnesium-based master alloys.
The refined titanium sponge and intermediate billets produced at Berezniki are transported to VSMPO’s primary smelting and mechanical processing facilities in Verkhnyaya Salda, Sverdlovsk region, to manufacture high-strength forgings, rolled sheets, and structural sub-assemblies.
The enterprise’s titanium alloys are critical structural materials utilized across Russian aerospace manufacturing, combat aviation, jet engine production, and missile systems.
Components fabricated from Avisma’s metals are integrated into fuselage airframes and turbine components for Su-35 and Su-57 fighter aircraft, fuselage mountings for tactical bombers, heavy armor assemblies, and missile airframes for cruise and ballistic platforms.
Beyond conventional defense hardware, specialized titanium castings and corrosion-resistant alloys from VSMPO-Avisma are supplied directly to Roscosmos for space rocket propulsion casings and to naval shipyards constructing nuclear-powered submarines.
Deep-tier asymmetric campaign against defense suppliers
The strike in Berezniki – located approximately 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukrainian borders in the Ural Mountains – forms part of an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign systematically targeting Russia’s deep-rear defense metallurgy and strategic chemical supply lines.
The incident in Perm region coincides with long-range drone strikes conducted across Siberia on Saturday, where unmanned platforms struck the Omsky Kauchuk chemical enterprise in Omsk – over 2,500 kilometers from Ukraine – igniting a large-scale blaze at a facility supplying synthetic rubbers and chemical binders used in solid rocket propellant for Iskander-M and intercontinental ballistic missile platforms.
Concurrently overnight into Sunday, Ukrainian strike drones engaged industrial and logistics infrastructure in central Belgorod, damaging the closed MegaGRINN commercial facility, while previous precision missile and drone interdictions hit the Proton defense microelectronics plant in Oryol and the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Samara region.

articles.title: Missiles Strike Energiya Defense Battery Plant in Yelets
articles.body:
Cruise missiles struck the “Energiya” defense-industrial enterprise in the city of Yelets in Russia’s Lipetsk region on Sunday, Oct. 25, targeting one of Russia’s foremost manufacturers of specialized power sources for guided missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, Radio Liberty and open-source intelligence monitors reported.
Lipetsk Region Governor Igor Artamonov confirmed an attack on the municipal industrial zone on Sunday, stating that municipal emergency services and defense specialists deployed to the impact zone, while refraining from identifying the enterprise in his initial dispatches.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to independent Russian monitoring outlet Astra and military open-source intelligence channels, incoming cruise missiles struck the production complex of the Energiya research and production enterprise.
Local monitoring channels and defense analysts suggested that the precision interdiction was executed using air-launched cruise missiles, potentially British-supplied Storm Shadow systems.
The facility functions as Russia’s largest scientific and industrial developer in the specialized field of autonomous chemical power sources, high-capacity accumulator batteries, and electrochemical energy units.
Specialized batteries for air defense, aviation, and drones
The Yelets plant occupies a critical, specialized niche within the Russia’s military-industrial complex, manufacturing electrochemical power components across military, aerospace, and civil aviation sectors.
Drones Strike Russian Titanium Producer Avisma in Urals
The enterprise develops and serially manufactures autonomous power supplies, specialized primary battery arrays, and compact lithium cells integrated directly into Russian strike drones, loitering munitions, and electronic control systems.
Energiya’s power units are essential components installed within surface-to-air missile systems, airborne avionics suites, naval combat vessels, and specialized guidance complexes for ballistic and cruise platforms.
Due to its strategic integration into the Kremlin’s defense-industrial supply chain, the Energiya enterprise is subjected to comprehensive international sanctions imposed by the US, the EU, the UK, Canada, Switzerland, Japan, Australia, and Ukraine.
The facility has previously been targeted in long-range interdiction strikes. In May 2025, an aerial strike ignited a major blaze across one of the primary production workshops, followed by a separate strike reported in January 2026.
Campaign against Russian military suppliers
The missile strike on Energiya in Lipetsk region coincides with an expanding Ukrainian precision campaign systematically targeting critical suppliers of specialized components, chemical precursors, and metallurgy across Russia’s rear defense sector.
Overnight into Sunday, long-range Ukrainian strike drones hit the “Avisma” chemical-metallurgical complex in Berezniki in the Perm region – located 1,500 kilometers (932 miles) away in the Ural Mountains – damaging a core facility of the world’s largest titanium producer vital for Russian combat aircraft, jet turbines, and missile fuselages.
Concurrently on Saturday, Ukrainian precision munitions struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical facility in Samara region and the Omsky Kauchuk chemical enterprise in Siberia, both of which manufacture synthetic rubbers and chemical binders essential for solid rocket propellant used in Iskander-M ballistic missiles and intercontinental systems.
Those operations followed confirmed precision Storm Shadow missile strikes on the Proton defense microelectronics complex in Oryol, which destroyed key production facilities supplying optoelectronics and power semiconductors for missile and air defense platforms.

2,000 Missiles in 48 Hours for the Middle East, Just 24 in 90 Days for Ukraine, Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine has received only 24 Patriot air defense interceptor missiles from the United States over the past 90 days, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, highlighting the limited supply of weapons needed to intercept Russian ballistic missiles as Kyiv continues to face large-scale aerial attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy in an interview with ABC News on October 24, the number of interceptors delivered to Ukraine stands in sharp contrast to the quantities used by the US and its Middle Eastern partners during recent military operations against Iran.
During the interview, Zelenskyy said that approximately 2,000 air defense missiles had been used in the first 48 hours of the war in the Middle East, compared with the 24 interceptors Ukraine received from its strategic partner over three months.
“We don’t cry, and we don’t scream, but this is very important. I am just trying to say that every missile matters.”
The Ukrainian president emphasized that every interceptor remains essential to protecting the country’s population and critical infrastructure from Russian missile attacks. Zelenskyy also raised concerns about delays in approving additional Patriot missile deliveries, including shipments already financed by European allies.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly not signed documents authorizing the transfer of a substantial number of Patriot interceptors, despite the missiles having already been paid for by Ukraine’s partners.
Ukrainian officials have described the delays as a possible form of political pressure, warning that interruptions in air defense supplies could leave civilian areas more vulnerable to Russian strikes.
Ukraine’s demand for Patriot interceptors remains significantly higher than current deliveries. Kyiv has previously indicated that it requires approximately 350 missiles per month to maintain sufficient protection against Russian ballistic threats.
Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has maintained that Washington has not changed its policy regarding military assistance to Ukraine under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative.
Rubio acknowledged that deliveries of interceptor missiles could experience delays because of competing demand from American allies worldwide and the need to maintain US military stockpiles.

articles.body:

Russia’s Missile Industry Takes a Double Hit as Ukraine Strikes Two Key Plants and Military Aircraft
Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed on October 24 that Ukrainian forces struck two Russian defense-related industrial facilities and an aircraft at a military airfield, targeting production chains supporting Russia’s cruise and ballistic missile programs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a statement published by the General Staff on October 24, the strikes targeted the Tolyattikauchuk chemical plant in Russia’s Samara region, the Proton-Electrotex electronics manufacturer in Orel, and an aircraft stationed at the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar region.
The military confirmed that the main production building of Proton-Electrotex was hit. The facility manufactures optoelectronic equipment and electronic components used in Russian weapons systems, including modules for S-71 Kover air-launched cruise missiles and inverter switches for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The company also participates in production chains supporting Russia’s Pantsir-S1 air defense systems and their modifications.
The General Staff said the damage could complicate the production of components for cruise and ballistic missiles used in Russian attacks against Ukrainian cities.
The strike follows reports from October 23 of explosions and smoke near the Proton-Electrotex facility in Orel. Social media accounts suggested that Ukrainian Flamingo missiles may have been involved, although the weapon used has not been officially confirmed.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical complex in Tolyatti overnight on October 24. The General Staff reported an explosion and fire in the vicinity of the facility.
Tolyattikauchuk manufactures synthetic rubber, monomers, hydrocarbon fractions, and high-octane gasoline additives. Some of its synthetic rubber products can be used as components in solid rocket propellants for tactical and ballistic missiles.
In addition to the industrial facilities, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed that an aircraft was struck at the Yeysk military airfield in Russia’s Krasnodar region.The type of aircraft was not specified, and the extent of the damage remains under assessment.
The General Staff has not disclosed the weapons used in the latest operations or provided a full assessment of damage to the two industrial facilities.
The Yeysk airfield was previously targeted on August 30, when Ukrainian forces struck the facility, triggering a fire and reported secondary explosions. Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed the strike, while satellite data detected a blaze extending from the aircraft parking area toward the runway.
