articles.title: Ex-Mossad chief Barnea intended for Iran to see Israel's operations to overwhelm IRGC
articles.body:
When the Mossad took the stunning move of publishing multiple videos in real time of its agents acting against the regime within Iran in June 2025, one of the main reasons was to overwhelm and confuse the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), former Mossad chief David Barnea has revealed.
Leaked on Sunday from comments he made to a closed audience at the Priority Summit this past Thursday.
On June 13, 2025, the Mossad released sensational and rare video footage of its co-lead role with the air force in Israel’s preemptive strike on Iran’s ballistic missiles and air defenses.
Three videos showed the Mossad targeting ballistic missile targets, air defense targets, and general preparations for the attacks (with the agents’ faces covered up).
From the perspective of the videos, it appeared that the Mossad used drones from inside Iran to attack various targets.
Iran had previously accused the Mossad of using drones to attack the Karaj facility in June 2021 as well as other operations.
Mossad's warehouse of drones used to sabotage Iran
It was later confirmed that the Mossad used an entire warehouse of drones to attack and sabotage Iran, along with helping with a large number of remote-controlled vehicles attacking regime targets, and a significant number of human agents on the ground also assisting in assassinations.
Although far more information was quickly publicized about the IDF’s actions, these videos gave readers a rare front-row and real-time seat into what normally were entirely clandestine operations which the Mossad would not even admit to.
Barnea said at the Priority Summit that the video was deliberately published to trigger mass arrests and make it more difficult for the IRGC to identify actual Israeli agents.
“One of the reasons we immediately released an official video on the morning of Operation Rising Lion, with the Mossad logo, was to protect the agents who were there,” Barnea said in a video which Yediot Ahronot shared, and regarding which the Jerusalem Post confirmed the authenticity. “We wanted to make sure they arrested so many people in Iran that they wouldn’t be able to distinguish the wheat from the chaff and would eventually release everyone,” adding that Iran did release all of the detainees.
IRGC arrested over 20,000 people on second day of war
The former Mossad chief said that the IRGC arrested 21,000 people on the second day of the fighting.
“You have to imagine that when you arrest 21,000 people, even if you’ve caught an agent or two, eventually you have to release them because everyone’s story will be the same: I was walking down the street, I was driving a car, they arrested me,” he said, emphasizing that the IRGC would have no way of knowing who was a real agent with such a vast number of detainees,
Barnea added that many of those arrested or executed by the IRGC as “Mossad agents” had nothing to do with the agency.
In addition, he said that nearly all of the Mossad agents were never caught, and at the end of the June 2025 operation, he even publicly taunted the IRGC, issuing a statement, “We will [continue to] be there, like we have been there.”
His explanation may close the book on the unexplained mystery of why the Mossad would have risked broadcasting some of its agents’ actions in real time during the June 2025 operation.
In September 2025, the Post reported exclusively that dozens of Mossad women penetrated Iran and were on the ground performing a variety of kinds of operations during Israel’s attacks on Tehran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs in June 2025.
While the Mossad does not want to bring too much attention to any one sub-group of potential spies, the Post’s impression was that the Mossad women of 2025 were doing more of every kind of spy role as compared to their sisters of yesterday.
In that same September report, the Post noted that Barnea sent hundreds of Mossad agents, or individuals being run by agents, into operations in Iran simultaneously. All of the varying groups of staff were highly coordinated.
The spy chief directed a project leading to a diverse spectrum of all of the different kinds of agents and backgrounds of those agents one could imagine.
On top of actual Israeli Mossad agents, the spy service has reached new levels in recruiting and training local dissident Iranian agents to act against the ayatollahs’ regime, the Post reported at the time.
While the early 2026 war with Iran is viewed by many as a mixed bag, the June 2025 war was viewed as the most successful Israeli operation of the last three years, along with the exploding beepers used against Hezbollah.

articles.title: Explainer-How Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy sites deepened the rift with Trump
articles.body:
Explainer-How Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy sites deepened the rift with Trump
WASHINGTON, Oct 25 - Relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy took a sharp downward turn in recent weeks, with each leader openly criticizing the other. The two have long had a testy relationship, but Trump's frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure triggered a crisis that Kyiv's supporters fear could threaten vital US support going forward.
Here's how the relationship soured:
WHAT IS THE HISTORY OF TRUMP-ZELENSKIY TENSIONS?
Trump has been skeptical of US involvement in Ukraine ever since his first term when, shortly after taking office in early 2017, he was asked to provide lethal aid to Ukraine and approved the sale of Javelin missiles to Kyiv.
“Everyone around him wanted him to do it, and they pushed him hard and he eventually signed off on selling them Javelins, very reluctantly,” said a former senior Trump administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. “He didn’t consider it a core US interest. It was a European issue.”
Trump's first major encounter with Zelenskiy came in a July 2019 phone call in which the Republican president asked the Ukrainian leader to investigate his Democratic rival Joe Biden and his son Hunter, in exchange for military support Congress had authorized.
That episode led to Trump's first impeachment. Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election.
Trump also has fostered a relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin that runs against the norms of US foreign policy but echoes his warm ties with authoritarian leaders Xi Jinping of China and North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.
“Trump has always wanted better relations with Russia,” the former official said.
WHAT DEEPENED THE RIFT BETWEEN THE TWO LEADERS?
Trump's current frustration centers on Kyiv's attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure.
Diesel prices have hit record highs since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, and global energy costs spiked. US lawmakers in Trump's Republican party face voter anger over inflation ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
On September 13, Trump began publicly calling on Ukraine to stop targeting diesel infrastructure. The following week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was also concerned that Ukraine had hit US-linked oil shipments.
Ukraine has refused to halt the strikes, saying its long-range drone campaign is its only viable response to nearly five years of Russian bombardment. Moscow was forced in July to ban diesel exports as part of a raft of measures to address domestic fuel shortages.
Angered by Zelenskiy’s defiance, Trump on October 9 announced a deal to buy diesel from Moscow, issuing a temporary general license that allows Russian diesel to reach the global market. He also waived sanctions on Russia authorized by a bill he signed into law in September.
Suriya Jayanti, a former US official who runs a power sector company in Ukraine, said Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s power grid have increased, despite Trump unilaterally announcing an energy ceasefire on October 11.
"It is clear to everyone in Kyiv that the goal is not actually an energy ceasefire, but it is really just an effort to hobble Ukraine and give Russia a decisive advantage," said Jayanti, who is also a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank.
HAS THE US THREATENED TO CUT OFF SUPPORT TO UKRAINE?
Zelenskiy has said Ukrainian military officials had been threatened by US counterparts, who said continuing the energy strikes would lead the US to cut off intelligence sharing. A US official familiar with the situation disputed Kyiv's account.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, the US official said there has been no increase in pressure on Ukraine.
“We don't have to pressure Zelenskiy. If he wants to make a deal he'll make a deal. I think Putin is putting a ton of pressure on him and he (Zelenskiy) is putting some pressure on Russia but Russia doesn't seem to be minding it as much even though they are getting hit."
On Thursday, Trump said he had asked SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the company's Starlink satellite system. Starlink's disruption temporarily hampered Kyiv's military drone operations and spurred fears that Kyiv would be left defenseless against Russia's attacks going into the winter.
WHAT IS THE STATUS OF MOSCOW-KYIV PEACE TALKS?
Peace efforts have continued but so far have not yielded tangible results.
At talks in Oslo on October 20, Ukraine presented new proposals, and Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner repeated Trump's demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
The next day, envoy Witkoff – a close friend of Trump's - met Putin in St. Petersburg. Putin agreed to release detained American Stephen Hubbard in what the two countries called a goodwill gesture.
Zelenskiy said on Friday that negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US would meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, a possible precursor to a meeting of the three countries’ leaders. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February. REUTERS

articles.title: Saudi Arabia turns to US AI system as Yemeni pressure mounts
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia turns to US AI system as Yemeni pressure mounts
TEHRAN – Failing to protect itself and its proxies in southern Yemen, Saudi Arbia has turned to an American-AI generated system to unsuccessfully counter Yemeni Armed Forces (YAF), also known as Ansarallah.
The war between Ansarallah and Saudi Arabia was resumed after Saudi Arabia on July 13 prevented a passenger plane carrying Ansarallah officials from landing in Sanaa by bombarding the airport, forcing the plane to land at Hodeidah International Airport.
After this reckless move, Ansarallah declared an eye-for-eye reprisal and started to target Saudi facilities, including airports and oil infrastructure. It also began targeting Saudi vessels in the Red Sea in response to the blockade of Yemen which has been in force for more than a decade.
Feeling helpless, Saudi Arabia has asked numerous allies for help. That includes the United States, even though media report that Donald Trump refused when Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman asked him to take direct military action against Ansarallah.
Ansarallah’s latest military campaign, which primarily began in September, has taken further control of Yemen's coast. So far, though, military campaigns against Ansarallah by Saudi Arabia, the United States and others have all failed.
Wary of Ansarallah, the U.S. is providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence, which includes a targeting tool that uses AI. A September report by U.S. broadcaster CNN, quoting several unnamed American officials, said that between 100 and 200 U.S. soldiers were in Saudi Arabia as part of new joint force command to facilitate this.
The U.S. personnel were helping the Saudis "use a targeting tool that allows military officers to see in real-time what is happening on the battlefield," CNN reported.
Officials said the system in Saudi Arabia was similar to that known as the Maven Smart System, or MSS for short, which the U.S. military has also used as it sought targets in Iran, Iraq and Syria.
MSS came out of what's known as Project Maven, the U.S. flagship artificial intelligence program for the military, first launched in 2017. MSS itself is an AI-enabled digital platform that "aggregates, organizes and visualizes vast streams of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data," analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington explained in a June text.
The software system identifies patterns in data coming from, for example, live satellite feeds or drone cameras and then labels potential targets such as possible rocket launchers, tanks or suspicious vehicle convoys.
Using the MSS dramatically speeds up what is known as "the kill chain" — that is, the time it takes to detect a target, decide if it's dangerous and then order a strike.
Up until recently, the long-simmering war in Yemen had been comparatively calm following an informal ceasefire negotiated in 2022.
Yemen’s Ansarallah has held large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2015. The pro-Saudi government and other groups held territory across the south and east.
There are certain technical issues users have noted with the MSS in the past that could also prove problematic in Yemen.
Ansarallah tends to be highly mobile, using truck-mounted ballistic missiles and small drone swarms as they operate from hills and canyons in rugged countryside. It's possible that fighters might be long gone before they can be attacked even with the help of AI-assisted targeting.
Though MSS is known to work best in relatively unpopulated areas, factors such as changes in desert terrain, dust storms, high wind, snowfall and dense foliage — and even deliberately planted decoys — can reduce its success rate.
There is also a worrying ethical aspect to shortening the kill chain. A human is always supposed to verify the target that the AI-assisted tool has identified and decide how to react.
But it doesn't always work that way. For example, among the sites MSS targeted in Iran on the first day of the war was a school. An American missile killed almost 200 people at a primary school in southern Iran, most of them children aged between seven and 12.
In its military campaign in Gaza, Israel has also used AI-assisted targeting. An Israeli system known as the Gospel, or Habsora, is the closest to MSS in the way it works.
But, as has been documented elsewhere, including by Israeli and British journalists and in the recent documentary Naza, the use of such AI targeting tools have also been highly problematic because of the numbers of civilian casualties that can result.
"On the one hand [in Gaza], AI has enhanced commanders' situational awareness, lessened the human costs of tunnel mapping, improved the speed of military strikes, and boosted the survivability of troops," analysts Frederic Wehrey and Andrew Bonney wrote for War on the Rocks, a specialist media outlet. "Yet the benefits afforded by such functions have been overshadowed by mounting civilian deaths reportedly resulting from this technology's safeguards being loosened or eliminated."
All of which is why Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist based in Australia who has researched the impact of Israel's AI-assisted technology, doesn't believe similar technology will lead to the defeat of Ansarallah.
"I don't think there's much evidence at all that using an AI tool is going to make much difference on the ground, except for causing huge amounts of civilian casualties," Loewenstein, who authored the book, "The Palestine Laboratory: How Israel Exports The Technology of Occupation Around the World," told DW. "And I think what the US and the Saudis will find is that the Houthis (Ansarallah) have an incredibly high tolerance level for destruction."

articles.title: Russia hits Ukrainian military logistics hubs – MOD
articles.body:
Russia hits Ukrainian military logistics hubs – MOD
Russian forces have launched an overnight attack targeting the Ukrainian military logistics network in the northeastern Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said. The list of targets included three hubs used to store and redistribute supplies for the armed forces and dual-use goods, the ministry said in a statement published on Sunday.
Separately, Russia also struck a bulk freighter in the Black Sea that was carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port city of Chernomorsk, the ministry added. The attacks were part of a broader operation that involved strikes on Ukrainian energy and transport infrastructure used to support the military, as well as drone storages and launch sites in a total of 159 locations over the past 24 hours.
Ukrainian officials confirmed strikes on the city of Kharkov, adding that an “industrial facility” was among the targets.
Russia has intensified its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial and logistics facilities in response to Kiev’s continued attacks on the Russian civilian and energy infrastructure. Moscow has repeatedly condemned the Ukrainian attacks as “terrorist acts” aimed at compensating for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the nation’s air defense systems intercepted a total of 532 Ukrainian drones during Sunday night alone. The drones were used in attempted attacks on more than two dozen Russian regions, the ministry stated.
Ukraine’s tactics have led to tension between Kiev and Washington. US President Donald Trump stated recently it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” and find a new person to negotiate peace instead of Vladimir Zelensky, whose presidential term expired more than two years ago. The American president also questioned the Ukrainian leader’s willingness to reach a deal with Moscow and criticized him for continued strikes on Russian oil refineries despite Washington’s repeated requests to stop.
Zelensky has said that Ukraine’s Western backers failed to provide advance warning about Russian ballistic missile launches twice in one week in October. He maintained however, that cooperation between Kiev and Washington had not been suspended, echoing Trump’s earlier remarks in which he said the US is “helping [Ukraine], and we are sharing intel.”
In the meantime, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Kiev of abusing his company’s Starlink civilian satellite internet network to launch offensive drone strikes. According to the US-based businessman, a “loophole” allowing the Ukrainian forces to do so was closed.

articles.title: 'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
articles.body:
'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
Russia has built an additional ring of air defense towers within 50 kilometers (30 miles) of Russian President Vladimir Putin's residence in Valdai, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) and OSINT analyst Jembob reported on Oct. 25.
Valdai is a small town in Russia's northwestern Novgorod Oblast. The town had a population of around 13,600 in 2025, according to Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
The defensive perimeter extends to the Khotilovo military base, which serves as an alternate landing site, and a secret biological laboratory on Lisiy Island, according to RFE/RL.
Satellite images indicate that the new perimeter encompasses both the military airfield in Khotilovo and the laboratory complex on Lisiy Island.
By October, air defense systems believed to be Pantsir or Tor units had been positioned south of Putin's residence, within the 50-kilometer (30-mile) zone.
No positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the perimeter, though additional sites could be established in the coming months, the report said.
One of the towers forming the outer defensive line was already in place by March 2026, on the grounds of the Khotilovo military air base. Putin reportedly uses the base regularly. A dedicated railway branch connects it to his Valdai residence, providing a direct train route, according to RFE/RL.
Other air defense sites have been established along the shores of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
RFE/RL published an investigation into the secret laboratory on the island on Sept. 3, around the same time construction began on two new air defense towers in the area.
The Kremlin accused Ukraine of attacking Putin's residence in Valdai with more than 90 drones on Dec. 29, 2025. Russian officials claimed the drones were carrying 6-kilogram (13-pound) high-explosive warheads, but claimed that air defenses had allegedly intercepted them all, with no casualties or damage reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Foreign Ministry denied the allegations, calling them a "lie." Kyiv also accused Moscow of fabricating the claims to undermine Ukraine's standing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration and derail ongoing peace efforts.
In early January 2026, the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) informed Trump that Ukraine had not targeted Putin's Valdai residence. U.S. intelligence assessed that Ukrainian forces had struck a military facility in the same region that night, but far from the Russian president's residence.

articles.title: Russian plant producing Iskander missile components hit in Yelets, 250 km from Ukraine – OSINT
articles.body:
Russian plant producing Iskander missile components hit in Yelets, 250 km from Ukraine – OSINT
The Energiya plant in the Russian city of Yelets in Lipetsk Oblast, which manufactures components for missile systems, was attacked by missiles on the afternoon of 25 October.
Source: analysts from Exilenova+, a Ukrainian OSINT community
Details: Exilenova+ reported that several missiles struck the facility, and smoke was seen across the plant's industrial zone following the hits. Storm Shadow cruise missiles were likely used in the attack on Energiya.
"Everything is burning there at the moment. The area around the strike has been cordoned off, and a large number of ambulances are heading to the plant," the analysts said.
Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov also reported an attack on Yelets. He said a strike had been recorded in the city's industrial zone.
Energiya PJSC specialises in developing and manufacturing electrochemical power sources, including accumulators, power cells and batteries. The facility is of strategic importance because its products are widely used in Russia's military-industrial complex, according to the War&Sanctions project run by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
Power cells and batteries manufactured at the Yelets plant are used in the production of Iskander-M cruise missiles, Zircon ballistic missiles, RM-48U missiles, 95Ya6 surface-to-air missiles for Pantsir air defence systems, and Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles.
Background:
- On 24 October, drones attacked the Omsky Kauchuk chemical plant in Russia, causing a fire at the facility.
- On the same day, Ukraine's defence forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast. An explosion and fire were reported following the strike.

articles.title: Why is the Middle East waiting out the Trump presidency?
articles.body:
There appears to be little prospect of lasting peace between Iran and the United States while Donald Trump remains in the White House. This is a view that an increasing number of serious actors across the region now seem to share. Eight months into Iran war, Washington has neither broken Tehran’s resolve nor found a clear path out. The president’s own remarks point to a narrowing set of options. Trump told TIME he does not believe peace with Iran is ever possible, a striking admission from the leader still expected to negotiate one.
Tehran, for its part, has set conditions it knows this administration cannot meet, insisting that sanctions and threats be lifted before talks resume and that not a single gram of enriched uranium leaves the country. Neither side is bargaining towards a settlement. Each is waiting for the political ground beneath the other to shift.
Trump’s problem is that the ground is shifting under him first, as the 3rd November midterms approach with his approval rating near 39 per cent and crude trading above 110 dollars a barrel. The House has voted three times to restrict his war powers in Iran, with Republican candidates in competitive seats now campaigning openly on ending the war to lower petrol prices. Facing a likely defeat, the president has promised no strikes before polling day while Central Command has reportedly been told to prepare for resuming major combat operations. Therefore, it is quite likely that Trump may order striking Iran even before the mid-term day.
Analysts have noted that a Republican defeat could strengthen this incentive, as a president with little left to lose at the ballot box faces fewer costs for escalation. Yet such strikes would do little damage control, since a Politico survey found 46 per cent of voters said ending the war before the election would not change their vote at all. Iran has meanwhile fortified its nuclear sites and warned that regional energy infrastructure would be targeted, so any parting blow risks sending oil prices even higher.
The president’s own inner circle appears to have read the same numbers and is quietly positioning itself for the aftermath. Vice President JD Vance, reportedly sceptical from the outset, has kept his distance and this week declined to endorse Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, his chief rival for 2028, spent the same week in India on a trip devoted largely to trade rather than Iran.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, by contrast, made an unannounced visit to Israel a day after Trump endorsed Netanyahu, keeping himself firmly in the frame. Commentators suggested as early as April that Hegseth was being set up as the fall guy should the war end badly. His visibility since has only reinforced that impression.
The Gulf states have reached the same conclusion. They are hedging accordingly against an American policy they no longer trust to last. The UAE joined the campaign against Iran in February, yet they opened a backchannel with Iranians lately after the realization that it is better to deal directly instead of relying on the US. Moreover, the UAE, by the virtue of being in support of the Saudis vis-à-vis Yemen, is trying to find a diplomatic way to lower tensions. It signals a striking reversal in barely eight months. Having absorbed thousands of Iranian missiles and drones, Abu Dhabi appears to be securing its own understandings before Washington’s next round begins.
Yemen shows how the burden is being shifted, since the United States has twice rebuffed Saudi requests for airstrikes against the Houthis and says it will not take kinetic action for now. Instead, the UAE has reportedly agreed to resume funding anti-Houthi forces in southern Yemen. This is an arrangement that lets Washington stay out while a partner carries the fight on its behalf.
Iran’s strategy rests on patience and its leaders appear confident they can absorb another year or so of American pressure before the political weather in Washington changes. Its posture towards Saudi Arabia fits this reading more closely than the images of burning airports suggest. Houthi strikes have killed at least 19 people at Saudi airports, and the Wall Street Journal has reported Revolutionary Guard officers helping to direct them. Yet within days of the deadliest attack, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called Riyadh to offer mediation with the Houthis and insist the crisis had no military solution.
The aim is not to destroy Saudi infrastructure but to convince the kingdom that American protection is unreliable and that any opening to Israel will carry a heavy price. Riyadh has begun to absorb that lesson, but the pressure is unlikely to ease while Trump remains in office and Tehran sees no reason to settle.
The real question is how Israel reacts to all this, both during the remainder of Netanyahu’s tenure and after it. Trump has endorsed Netanyahu so he can help “finish the job” against Iran, and Israel has reportedly asked that any renewed strikes wait until after its 27 October vote. Polls give Netanyahu’s coalition fewer than 50 of the 61 seats needed to govern, raising the prospect of a weakened caretaker with every reason to keep the Iran file burning.
A successor led by Gadi Eisenkot would hardly soften Israel’s line on the Iranian nuclear programme, but it might be less willing to tie national strategy to American president’s fortunes. Should Israel strike alone after an American exit, Gulf hedging would only accelerate and normalisation with Riyadh would recede further from view.
Tehran and the Gulf have made their calculations. Both now wait for a different figure in the Oval Office.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian plant supplying batteries for ballistic missiles and glide bombs with Storm Shadow missiles, OSINT reports – another hit on Russia’s weapons supply chain
articles.body:
Ukraine reportedly struck the Energiya plant in Yelets, Russia’s Lipetsk Oblast, with UK-supplied Storm Shadow cruise missiles on 25 October, according to the OSINT channel Exilenova+.
The plant manufactures batteries and power sources used in Russian weapons systems, including Iskander and Kinzhal missiles, air defense systems, and guided aerial bombs, according to Exilenova+. The reported strike targeted a facility that supplies components for Russia’s military-industrial complex as Moscow continues its war against Ukraine.
According to Exilenova+, Energiya is Russia's only producer of batteries for glide bomb planning and correction modules, as well as a key supplier of specialized power sources for several missile systems.
Storm Shadow missiles reportedly hit plant buildings
Exilenova+ reported multiple missile impacts at the Energiya plant, sharing footage and photos showing explosions, thick smoke, and fires at the facility. The channel later reported that the plant was still burning and that the surrounding area had been cordoned off, with numerous ambulances heading to the site.
Dnipro OSINT reported that at least two missiles struck two buildings at the plant.
The Energiya plant is located in Yelets, approximately 250 km (150 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Plant produces components for Russian weapons
According to Dnipro OSINT, Energiya specializes in developing and manufacturing chemical power sources. Its products are used in several Russian weapons systems, including Iskander-K and Iskander-M missiles, Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles, Zircon missiles, and Pantsir air defense systems. The plant also supplies power sources for UMPB D-30SN guided aerial bombs.
Many of these weapons are used in Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, killing civilians and destroying residential buildings and civilian infrastructure.
UN food aid warehouse in Dnipro struck by Russian Iskander missile, impacting supplies for 130,000 people
Dnipro OSINT said the plant had been attacked at least four times before the 25 October strike.
The strike comes two days after a reported Ukrainian Storm Shadow missile attack on the Proton electronics plant in Russia’s Oryol on 23 October, which produces electronic components used in Russian weapons systems, including Iskander-M ballistic missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.

articles.title: CENTCOM reportedly has plans for Iran strikes: Will Trump approve them?
articles.body:
CENTCOM reportedly has plans for Iran strikes: Will Trump approve them?
US media reporting that Pentagon has drawn up plans to renew strikes after November 3 midterm elections, but analysts question what another bombing campaign could achieve.
The US military has drawn up options for renewed attacks on Iran, according to the Washington-based website The Hill, raising the prospect of another round of major fighting in a war approaching its eighth month.
Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US forces in the Middle East, has plans ready for follow-up strikes if authorised by the White House, the outlet reported. It also said military planners had prepared several options for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The report focused on possible attacks after the November 3 US midterm elections. But President Donald Trump suggested on Saturday that the United States could strike as soon as “tomorrow”, while also holding out the possibility of a “big, beautiful” agreement with Tehran.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, accused Washington of derailing negotiations but said efforts to reach an agreement should continue. With both sides warning of further attacks, could the conflict tip back into full-scale war? Here is what we know.
What are the plans?
The latest reporting suggests military preparations are advancing, although it remains unclear which options Trump might approve or when. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the Pentagon had instructed CENTCOM to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations. Its sources said a renewed campaign could target Iranian energy facilities, infrastructure and nuclear sites.
Those preparations do not amount to an order to attack. The decision ultimately rests with Trump, whose public statements continue to leave room for both military action and negotiations.
Meanwhile, on Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the US and Israel have drawn up joint plans for an attack on Iran after the midterm elections. The reports come alongside US warnings about alleged Iranian threats to American personnel overseas. An intelligence memo sent on Friday by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran had “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel”, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and elsewhere.
The Department of State has ordered staffing reductions at several regional embassies amid the warnings. The publicly reported memo did not identify specific targets or establish when any alleged attacks might occur.
Trump has added to the uncertainty. At a rally on Friday, he said Washington “may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the codename of the US-Israeli military operation against Iran that began on February 28. On Saturday, he declined to disclose the timing of any possible attack while suggesting one could come as early as Sunday.
Julie Norman, associate fellow at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera the preparations served both as short-term posturing and a possible longer-term military objective next month. “With Trump, I think he is always keeping options on the table, but I think this particular drawing up of plans is an immediate posturing deterrent, but also a very real option after the midterms,” she said.
It comes as the US is deploying a third aircraft carrier strike group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, along with roughly 10,000 additional soldiers and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East by the end of November.
How has Iran responded?
Tehran has combined calls for further negotiations with warnings that renewed US attacks would bring a wider response. “We were having negotiations, the cowards [Americans] messed everything up,” Pezeshkian said in remarks broadcast on Saturday, before adding that efforts to conclude the agreement should continue.
Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf will also miss the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum in New Delhi, according to the Iranian Embassy in India. The embassy cited “unforeseen circumstances” without elaborating.
On Sunday, Iran’s army also said it had shot down a US-developed LUCAS drone over the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
The Reuters news agency has reported, quoting Iranian security officials, that Tehran has drawn up plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of a resumption of US and Israeli attacks.
The incident followed Iranian claims that seven oil tankers had caught fire or sustained damage in and around the Strait of Hormuz earlier this week, while on Wednesday, Iran also announced what it describes as a shift towards an “offensive” military doctrine, warning that countries hosting bases used in US attacks could become targets.
“Our defence doctrine was previously defensive; we used to say that if a country attacks us, we will respond. Now we say that if a country attacks us, we will both respond and launch an offensive,” Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman Hossein Mohebi said.
The warning raises the prospect of a confrontation spreading further across the region, with energy infrastructure and countries aligned with Washington potentially exposed. “Iran is also drawing up its own target lists to include energy infrastructure and US-aligned states,” Norman said.
“So I would say both parties are certainly very prepared for another round of escalation and projecting preparedness to each other.”
“In the meantime, there is a very high risk of miscalculation by either side, a very high risk of rapid escalation.”
October has become the worst month for attacks on ships since the war began in February, with more than 120 attacks reported so far.
Would another attack serve Trump’s interests?
The timing is politically sensitive, with Trump facing pressure to avoid renewed escalation before the US midterm elections, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pushing for an attack as his support dwindles in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s election.
It comes after Netanyahu said overthrowing Iran’s government remains Israel’s “primary objective”.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies in Qatar, said recent developments pointed towards renewed fighting rather than a diplomatic breakthrough. “There is a lot of signalling, a lot of posturing suggesting that we are headed for another round of fighting,” he told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to Hegseth’s recent visit to Israel, and Washington’s reported withdrawal of personnel from regional diplomatic and military sites. “All of that would suggest that the US and Israel are planning [another round of attacks] on Iran, either soon or very soon,” he said.
“One of the fears is this next round of fighting could actually be more dangerous, more catastrophic than the previous round.”
Norman added that while the US president may be eyeing up a strike on Iran after the midterms, “the big question for Trump from military advisers is – what would a further round of escalation bring that the other rounds didn’t?”
“What would these strategies do to force Iran to the negotiating table? And I don’t think there has been a clear answer to that.”

articles.title: Russia Launche 1,600 Bombs and 2,300 Drones Over Past Week
articles.body:
Russian forces launched approximately 1,600 guided aerial bombs, nearly 2,300 strike drones, and 48 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Oct. 25.
In a statement on Facebook and reported by state news agency Ukrinform, Ukraine’s head of state outlined the human and material toll of the relentless aerial campaign, emphasizing that strikes have inflicted fatal and non-fatal civilian casualties on a near-daily basis.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“During this week alone, Russia launched around 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistics, and almost 2,300 strike drones against Ukraine,” Zelensky stated.
“Unfortunately, almost every day there are dead and wounded from these brutal strikes.”
Overnight damage across nine regions
Zelensky highlighted the operational breadth of recent Russian strikes, confirming that overnight bombardments damaged critical infrastructure and civilian facilities across nine administrative regions.
Adversary munitions struck thermal power plants, electrical substations, coal mining enterprises, grain storage facilities, commercial shopping centers, and a postal terminal.
The president reviewed the casualties caused by the weekend’s standoff attacks, pointing to the deadly drone strike on the city of Synelnykove in Dnipropetrovsk region, which killed four civilians and wounded 22 others, including an 11-year-old girl.
Russia Targets Epicentr Stores Across 4 Cities in Under 24 Hours
Zelensky also referenced the strike on a five-story residential building in Vinnytsia that injured six people and forced the evacuation of an adjacent nursing home, alongside the assault on Kharkiv, where Russian forces struck a construction hypermarket and subsequently launched a secondary strike targeting arriving emergency rescue workers.
Calls for air defense deliveries
Addressing the geopolitical dimension of the ongoing bombardments, Zelensky observed that Moscow’s intensified attacks reflect its actual response to international diplomatic initiatives and efforts to end its isolation.
“This is precisely how Russia reacts to diplomacy and de-isolation,” Zelensky emphasized, stressing that Western partners must not permit military assistance to decline while diplomatic tracks are explored.
The president urged European allies to expedite defense support, calling specifically for the immediate release of surface-to-air interceptors that have already received political clearance from partner governments.
“It is necessary to unblock the supplies of Patriot interceptors already agreed upon by the Europeans,” Zelensky said.
“It is necessary to further support Ukrainian combat aviation to protect against jet-powered Shaheds. Every such defense package, especially ahead of winter, helps save lives.”

articles.title: Medvedev called on Trump to "get rid of" Zelenskyy using the CIA and the U.S. military
articles.body:
Medvedev called on Trump to "get rid of" Zelenskyy using the CIA and the U.S. military
Kyiv • UNN
Dmitry Medvedev suggested that Trump involve the U.S. military and the CIA against Zelenskyy. He provided no evidence for his accusations.
Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev issued yet another threat against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. This time, the former Russian president suggested that Donald Trump instruct the U.S. military and the CIA to "deal with" the Ukrainian leader. The Moscow Times reports this, writes UNN.
Details
In his post, Medvedev complained that Zelenskyy allegedly insults Trump, demands money and weapons from the United States, and refuses to accept proposals for peace talks. The Russian official was also displeased by Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries in the Russian Federation.
Medvedev also accused Zelenskyy of embezzling American aid and creating a threat of a nuclear conflict between Russia and NATO. He presented no evidence of these accusations in the statement cited.
Medvedev decided to advise Trump on how to act against Zelenskyy
In the opinion of the deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, the Ukrainian president allegedly causes greater harm to American interests than Venezuela, Cuba, and Iran combined.
What should Trump do with this "son of a bitch" of his? The answer can be found in American history. He should simply summon the secretary of war and the CIA director and instruct them to correct this unfortunate misunderstanding… The method, place, and means do not matter
It is noteworthy that a representative of the Russian leadership, whose country launched a full-scale war against Ukraine, is now suggesting that U.S. intelligence agencies target the president of a state defending itself against this aggression.
This is not Medvedev’s first statement of this kind. Earlier, he had already proposed applying a "Venezuelan scenario" to Ukraine, meaning the forcible removal of the head of state.
Despite the loudness of the new threat, Medvedev has no authority to issue orders to the U.S. military or intelligence agencies. Therefore, for now, his proposal remains yet another public drunken outburst by a Russian official, rather than evidence of any plans by Washington.

articles.title: The Former General Who Could End the Netanyahu Era
articles.body:
Gadi Eisenkot’s office is small and sparsely furnished. There are no medals on display, no photographs with foreign dignitaries or political luminaries, none of the trappings of a decorated general who rose to become chief of staff of Israel’s military. The space, tucked inside a commercial building in the Tel Aviv suburb of Ramat HaSharon, is conspicuously devoid of ostentation.
Beside his desk sit three photographs. One is of his son Gal, who was killed fighting in Gaza in Dec. 2023, two months after the war began. Another is a family portrait taken during a visit to Washington, D.C., years earlier, a picture of a family still whole, before the war shattered it. The third shows Gal next to one of his closest friends from their military unit, who was also killed in combat. “He was a settler,” Eisenkot says of his son’s friend. The image conveys a snapshot of contemporary Israel: the son of a centrist military commander and a young man from a West Bank settlement, products of different worlds, serving and dying alongside one another.
As we speak, Eisenkot, dressed in his trademark black polo and black pants, pauses to pick up the photographs. He recalls the days after his son’s death. After three nights of sitting shiva, the Jewish mourning ritual, he left his grieving family to attend a meeting of Benjamin Netanyahu’s war cabinet. “I decided to go forward,” he says.
Now Eisenkot hopes to move not only himself forward but his country. The former general has emerged as a leading challenger to Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. Polls suggest a close contest, with Eisenkot seeking to assemble a coalition capable of ending Netanyahu’s rule three years after he presided over the worst security failure in Israel’s history, launched the war in Gaza, and led the country into deepening international isolation.
Eisenkot has cultivated a reputation for integrity, competence, and personal rectitude, forging relationships across Israel’s fractured political spectrum. But perhaps his most powerful political asset is his devastating personal loss. In a country scarred by the trauma of Oct. 7 and the war that followed, Eisenkot’s grief is familiar to countless Israelis. His effort to persevere mirrors a nation’s struggle.
The Oct. 27 election will be more than a referendum on Netanyahu. It will test whether Israelis are prepared to chart a different course after three years of bloodshed, recriminations, and cultural fracture. The country is deeply polarized, increasingly castigated by the rest of the world, and confronting a resurgence of antisemitism. Voters will determine not only who governs Israel but what kind of nation Israel will become—and whether its next leader can begin to heal the divisions that have left the world’s only Jewish state facing one of the gravest crises in its history.
Netanyahu, of course, can never be counted out. The consummate political survivor, he has weathered scandals, electoral defeats, and corruption charges. His credibility has suffered, but many Israelis still regard him as the only leader who can protect them in a dangerous region. Eisenkot could assemble a coalition with other opposition figures, including former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Lieberman, and Yair Golan. Netanyahu would depend on the far-right parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, whose ultra-nationalist politics have found a receptive audience among younger right-wing Israelis.
Israel’s fragmented parliamentary system offers no guarantee of a decisive outcome. Negotiations could drag on for weeks, or fail altogether, sending Israelis back to the polls. Eisenkot tells me he will not serve in a unity government with Netanyahu under any circumstances. He has framed his ambitions around nothing less than the sustenance of the Zionist enterprise: the ability of Jews to live safely in a state of their own in their ancestral homeland. In his telling, that means confronting the threat from Iran; restoring Israel’s standing in the world; preserving the country’s character as a Jewish democracy; and finding an accommodation with the Palestinians, who lay claim to the same land and have their own aspirations to self-determination.
“What holds the country together is the Jewish and democratic ethos of the majority of Israelis,” says Yossi Klein Halevi, a bestselling Israeli author and senior fellow at the Shalom Hartman Institute in Jerusalem. “That's what we're going to have to try to repair. That is really what Eisenkot is offering the country.”
For Eisenkot, the challenge is not merely to replace Netanyahu but to lead Israel beyond the trauma that has consumed it since Oct. 7. He sees a country caught between the imperative to protect itself and the need to recover the democratic values, national solidarity, and international legitimacy that are essential to its survival. “I feel like it’s a historic mission—to save the state of Israel,” he says, invoking his son and the many others who died defending the nation. “We owe it to them to be worthy of the sacrifice they made.”
On Oct. 7, 2023, Eisenkot awoke shortly after 6 a.m., stirred by nothing more than his circadian rhythm. When he turned on the television, he saw the first images of a catastrophe unfolding a short drive south of his home. Thousands of Hamas-led militants were pouring into southern Israel by land, air, and sea. They rampaged through kibbutzim and the streets of Sderot, descended on the Nova music festival, where they murdered civilians, raped women, desecrated the bodies of the dead, and dragged hundreds of hostages back into Gaza. Many filmed themselves carrying out the atrocities, celebrating the carnage as it unfolded. Desperate Israelis called the authorities, pleading for help that would not arrive for hours. By the time security forces regained control, entire communities had been devastated by the worst slaughter of Jews since the Holocaust.
Eisenkot’s son Gal, 25, was staying at the family home in Herzliya, outside of Tel Aviv, rather than his apartment near Tel Aviv University, where he was studying bioinformatics. He had come home for the holiday of Simchat Torah. Eisenkot woke him. “Gal, come to see the TV,” he said. “There are trucks of Hamas inside Sderot. This means war. Where is your military equipment?”
Gal had completed his compulsory service and was now a reservist, trained as a combat medic. Eisenkot drove him to his unit’s base, where lines of cars were already forming as reservists converged. “I knew right away that Israel, that the world, would never be the same,” Eisenkot says.
Four days later, with a ground invasion of Gaza looming, Netanyahu asked Eisenkot to join a small war cabinet. Eisenkot had served under Netanyahu as chief of the general staff from Feb. 2015 to Jan. 2019, but the two men were now political adversaries. Netanyahu had hoped to project unity to a divided public, much of which had come to distrust or despise him. After months of mass demonstrations against his efforts to curtail the power of the judiciary, he sought to rally the country behind the coming war.
One of Eisenkot’s first priorities in the war cabinet was to prevent the opening of a second front against Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed Shiite militant group in Lebanon. Some of Netanyahu’s senior ministers, particularly Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, favored launching a preemptive offensive against Hezbollah, despite objections from the Biden Administration. Eisenkot argued that Israel needed to concentrate its military resources on defeating Hamas in the south before embarking on another major conflict. On that question, he prevailed.
On another matter, one he considered even more urgent, Netanyahu was less receptive. Hamas had abducted 251 people on Oct. 7, and Eisenkot believed securing their release should take precedence over a full-scale military campaign. It was, in his view, a fundamental obligation of the state, part of the covenant between a country and its citizens. Once Israel plunged into a prolonged ground war, he feared, the prospects of recovering the hostages alive would diminish. “My idea was to do the hostage deal, and after that, defeat Hamas,” Eisenkot tells me.
Netanyahu chose a different course. Israel launched a ground invasion following an extensive aerial bombardment of Hamas’s military infrastructure, including its vast network of subterranean tunnels. Hamas had embedded military facilities and weapons in densely populated areas, deliberately exposing civilians to grave danger. The military campaign that ensued has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.
Two months into the war, Eisenkot suffered a catastrophe of his own. He was at a military headquarters, studying a satellite map showing the positions of Israeli battalions near some of the fiercest fighting in Gaza. Fifteen minutes later, a major general who had once served under his command approached him.
“Gadi, come to me,” the officer said. “Gal is critically injured. Go home”
Eisenkot had spent more than four decades in the Israeli military. He knew what those words meant. If his son were still alive, he would have been told to go to the hospital, not home. “I understood he was dead,” he tells me.
Gal died in combat alongside his friend Eyal Berkowitz, a young man from a West Bank settlement. It was Berkowitz whose photograph Eisenkot had shown me in his office, standing beside Gal.
Thousands attended Gal’s funeral, which was broadcast on national television. Across the country, Israelis watched one of their most decorated commanders mourn the loss of his own son. Eisenkot delivered a eulogy, his voice trembling. “I promise you that we will continue to be a united and happy family, so that your sacrifice and that of the other fallen will not be in vain and that we will be worthy of it,” he said. “I salute you, beloved son.”
Three days later, Eisenkot returned to Netanyahu’s war cabinet. He watched as Netanyahu’s prosecution of the war turned Israel into a pariah state. Images circulated daily on social media of children killed as collateral damage in strikes on Hamas targets. Netanyahu resisted allowing aid into the Strip. The world accused Israel of using starvation as a weapon of war and committing war crimes against a trapped population of 2 million.
He recalls his final meeting with Netanyahu, in late June 2024, when the prime minister appeared before a special intelligence committee in the Knesset. Eisenkot pressed him on how he intended to end the war. “What is your exit plan?” he asked. Netanyahu offered none, Eisenkot says, insisting instead that Israel would continue fighting until it achieved “total victory.”
Eisenkot reached into his briefcase and pulled out a book: Master of the Game: Henry Kissinger and the Art of Middle East Diplomacy, Martin Indyk’s 2021 study of Kissinger’s statecraft. Indyk, who served in senior diplomatic roles under Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, was a friend of Eisenkot’s and a longtime critic of Netanyahu. “Have you read this?” Eisenkot asked. Netanyahu said he had not. Eisenkot urged him to do so, arguing that military force without a diplomatic strategy could not deliver a lasting victory.
“Gadi,” Eisenkot recalls Netanyahu replying, “I have a different view about the meaning of the word strategy.”
Eisenkot was enraged by Netanyahu’s refusal to prioritize the hostages. The suspicion among Netanyahu’s critics was that he feared a deal would fracture his coalition, potentially forcing elections that could remove him from power and trigger an inquiry into the failures of Oct. 7––much like the Agranat Commission, established after the 1973 Yom Kippur War, that led to the downfall of Golda Meir. In Eisenkot’s telling, Netanyahu put the preservation of his own power above the lives he was entrusted to protect. “He neglected them,” Eisenkot says.
A spokesperson for the prime minister did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
On June 9, 2024, Eisenkot resigned from the emergency government, ending his eight-month effort to influence the war from within. His departure, alongside that of Benny Gantz, effectively ended the national unity arrangement and precipitated the dissolution of the war cabinet. But the war was not finished exacting its toll on Eisenkot’s family. One nephew had already died fighting in Gaza on the same day of his son’s funeral. Another was killed 11 months later.
Over the next two years, Netanyahu presided over a succession of extraordinary military operations. Israel killed Yahya Sinwar, the Hamas leader who helped mastermind the Oct. 7 massacre, and Ismail Haniyeh, the group’s longtime political chief. It assassinated Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah and dealt devastating blows to the Iranian-backed militia in Lebanon, including through an audacious operation that turned thousands of its members’ pagers into explosive devices. After Donald Trump returned to the White House, Netanyahu persuaded the president to join Israel’s 12-day war against Iran in June 2025, with U.S. forces striking three of Iran’s principal nuclear facilities.
But the military triumphs told only part of the story. For two years, the war in Gaza devastated the Palestinian enclave, killed tens of thousands of people, and left Israeli hostages languishing in captivity. In October 2025, under intense pressure, Netanyahu agreed to a ceasefire and hostage-exchange deal that halted the fighting and secured the release of the remaining living hostages. “Netanyahu dragged it” out, Eisenkot says. “President Trump pushed him to do it.”
Months later, the confrontation with Iran entered a more perilous phase. Netanyahu helped persuade Trump to join a broader war against the Islamic Republic, a conflict that grew difficult to end and intensified criticism of Israel in the United States, including among elements of the American right. Around 60% of U.S. adults now hold an unfavorable view of Israel, according to a 2026 Pew survey.
Now, for the first time since Oct. 7, Netanyahu must face the electorate. Eisenkot thinks Netanyahu has done little to help Israel recover, instead perpetuating the trauma, cultivating a siege mentality and an atmosphere of never-ending conflict that allows him to cast himself as the indispensable wartime leader. “I don’t know how Netanyahu wants to close the story,” Eisenkot says.
He decided he would try to write the ending himself.
Eisenkot’s strategy has been to assemble a broad coalition. To his right, he envisions Bennett and the secular nationalist Liberman; to his left, Golan, leader of the Democrats, the successor to the historic Labor Party, and Lapid, the former television host who briefly served as prime minister. “I told them, let’s build a big party,” Eisenkot says.
He held a series of talks with Bennett about the prospect of running together, but ultimately declined, calculating that separate campaigns would give the opposition bloc a better chance of expanding their support. Instead, Eisenkot chose to lead his own party, Yashar. Bennett subsequently joined forces with Lapid. “I thought I had the ability to unite Israel, unite this divided country,” Eisenkot says, citing his military experience and relationships across the political spectrum. “It’s not from arrogance but from deep commitment to bring change and defeat Netanyahu.”
Eisenkot’s background also carries significance. Born in Tiberias to Moroccan Jewish immigrants and raised in the southern port city of Eilat, he belongs to Israel’s Mizrahi community, Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent who have long faced discrimination from the country’s predominantly Ashkenazi establishment. If elected, he would become Israel’s first Mizrahi prime minister.
Eizenkot has campaigned on restoring public trust in government, strengthening Israel’s security, and preserving its foundation as a Jewish democracy. He has pledged to dismantle illegal outposts in the West Bank and crack down on extremist Jewish settlers who terrorize Palestinians, expand military or civilian national service across Israeli society, confront the threat from Iran, pursue a political resolution to the Palestinian conflict, repair Israel’s frayed relationships abroad, and restore national unity.
Travel through the country and the psychological scars of Oct. 7 are difficult to miss. They surface in the impatience of drivers, the intensity of political arguments, the restless energy of a society still living in the shadow of a nightmare. The country seems suspended in its aftermath, unable to separate the horrors of the past from the anxieties of the present. In some ways, it is still Oct. 8, 2023.
During our interview, Eisenkot and I discuss Bessel van der Kolk, the Harvard psychiatrist whose bestselling book, The Body Keeps the Score, explores how overwhelming experiences can leave people psychologically trapped in the past. Trauma, van der Kolk argues, can persist long after the danger has passed, disrupting the ability to integrate painful memories and move forward.
Eisenkot believes Netanyahu has purposefully made that process harder. Nearly three years on, Israel has yet to establish a state commission of inquiry into the failures that allowed the attack to happen. Without an authoritative accounting, Eisenkot argues, the country cannot fully reckon with the catastrophe. He pledges to establish such a commission within his first 14 days in office, with a mandate to investigate not only Oct. 7 but the decade of decisions that preceded it, including his own tenure leading the military.
He points to widespread suspicions that the attack involved some form of betrayal from within, a belief he attributes partly to Netanyahu’s efforts to shift responsibility onto military and intelligence officials. Netanyahu and members of his family have promoted disputed allegations that security officials deliberately withheld warnings before the Oct. 7 attack, including the claim that they failed to wake the prime minister as Hamas launched its assault—part of a broader effort by Netanyahu and his allies to shift responsibility for the security failures onto the military and intelligence establishment.
Recent polls show a close contest, with Yashar running ahead of Likud. But neither Netanyahu’s right-wing alliance nor the parties seeking to replace him appear assured of the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
“I think the chances for a unity government are high because we will be more than happy to have Eisenkot joining our coalition,” says Ohad Tal, a Knesset Member running with Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party. “If the other side will have a majority with the Arabs, God save us.”
Forming an alternative majority could require support from Arab parties, a fraught prospect in Israeli politics. Eisenkot will not commit to bringing them into his government. Instead, he has set four conditions for any coalition partner: recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; adherence to the principles of its Declaration of Independence; acceptance of a national-service obligation for all citizens, with civilian alternatives to military service; and agreement that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be dismantled. None of the Arab parties has yet to accept the latter tenet.
“I understand that in the Israeli system we must have a big bloc,” Eisenkot says. “It’s a huge challenge. I’m doing my best from morning till night. I’m convinced we’ll defeat Netanyahu.”
If Eisenkot succeeds, he says, he will break with Netanyahu’s defining political method: cultivating a siege mentality that pits Israel against the world. “The main challenge is to break Netanyahu’s method with them and us,” Eisenkot tells me. “This is poison to our society.”
Nowhere is that more consequential than in the United States, where support for Israel has deteriorated, particularly among younger Americans. “Netanyahu knows the United States better than all of us, but today he can’t improve Israel’s relationship with the U.S.,” Eisenkot says. “He may have a good relationship with the administration today, but the situation in universities, with American Jewry, with the bipartisan relations, are at their lowest.”
One of Eisenkot’s proposals is to gradually wean Israel off American military assistance. He believes the dependence has become a source of friction in Washington, and runs counter to the Zionist ideal of a Jewish state capable of guaranteeing its own security. “Maybe it will take five to 10 years,” he says, “and it is our interest to do it.”
Eisenkot opposes the establishment of a Palestinian state, a goal long championed by much of the international community. But he also recognizes the profound danger of a one-state future: Israel would face a choice between granting millions of Palestinians citizenship and voting rights, which would end its Jewish majority, or denying them those rights, which would undermine its claim to be a democracy. He wants to prevent the vision of permanent Israeli control advanced by Smotrich and Ben-Gvir. “Smotrich’s vision for one state will be the end of our country,” Eisenkot says.
To avert that outcome, Eisenkot tells me he favors some form of separation in the West Bank, with a reformed Palestinian Authority assuming greater responsibility for Palestinian self-government while Israel retains military control over the territory. His approach to Gaza is different. He endorses the framework of Trump’s 20-point peace plan, which calls for a technocratic Palestinian administration to govern the enclave and envisions a conditional pathway to Palestinian statehood.
“We have two options: the 20 points of President Trump, or to use force,” Eisenkot says. “I prefer the diplomatic option—and I believe I can do it. But if not, I know how to dismantle Hamas with force.”
For all his confidence in working with Trump, Eisenkot and his advisers were surprised when the president endorsed Netanyahu. Trump had previously passed up opportunities to do so, including in an interview with TIME. Some of his closest Middle East advisers, including his son-in-law Jared Kushner, had grown frustrated with the Israeli leader. According to people familiar with the discussions, Fox News host Mark Levin and U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee urged Trump to back Netanyahu in the closing days of the campaign. “Israeli society is independent and will make its own decision,” Eisenkot says. “I have no doubt Trump will accept every democratic choice in Israel.”
Netanyahu’s political operation has circulated a stream of AI-generated videos attacking Eisenkot, including one depicting him in a field approaching a young Israeli soldier who bears a striking resemblance to his dead son. Instead of embracing the soldier, the figure resembling Eisenkot pushes him aside and embraces Mansour Abbas. “I felt contempt,” Eisenkot says when we discuss the video. “That is the lowest he could go.” The invective has only continued. Yinon Magal, a Channel 14 host and pro-Likud commentator, called Eisenkot a “monkey” on air. Netanyahu waited days before describing it as “highly inappropriate.”
Eisenkot sees the election as a test of whether Israel can preserve the democratic and national ideals of the Zionist movement or drift further from them. “My goal is that the Israeli people will be united and proud of their country,” he says. “That global Jewry will be proud of Israel as the national home of the Jewish people.” Many fear an exodus of Israelis should Netanyahu hang on. A Channel 12 poll in July found that 23% said they or any of their relatives would leave if the Israeli premier is reelected.
Eisenkot lacks Netanyahu’s rhetorical flair, polished English, and decades on the world stage. But he argues those advantages have grown less useful as Netanyahu grows increasingly polarizing, at home and abroad. For many critics of Israel, particularly younger ones, the distinction between the country and its longtime leader has become difficult to discern. “We need to return to speaking about sharing the same values,” Eisenkot says. “Nobody speaks about values right now. Everything is about interest, power, more power, and more power.”
As our interview draws to a close, Eisenkot returns once more to the subject of trauma, the force that has shaped his own life and, he believes, the fate of his country. “Netanyahu is unwilling to show the courage needed to end the war from a position of strength,” he says. “It will take years to close the trauma, but we must start now.”
- With Reporting by Liam Forberg

articles.title: Russia’s once-feared Lancet kamikaze drone is losing its edge
articles.body:
- A Russian unit launched about 100 Lancet drones over three months and hit only three targets, pro-Russian militant Pavel Gubarev said.
- He put the cost at about $3.7 million to $6.1 million, saying Ukrainian air defenses stopped most drones.
A Russian drone unit fired about 100 Lancet loitering munitions over three months and hit only three targets, according to pro-Russian militant Pavel Gubarev, who said Ukrainian air defenses brought down most of the rest. The account points to a sharp drop in the effectiveness of one of Russia’s most widely used strike drones, Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi reported.
Gubarev said the drones were launched by a team from the Russian “Sparta” unit commanded by Senior Lt. Kirill Ozerov, call sign “Nevsky,” over a three-month period that began in mid-June. He did not name the section of the front where the unit operates.
The three targets hit were a self-propelled artillery gun, an infantry dugout and a roadside shop, Gubarev said. Ukrainian air defenses neutralized most of the remaining drones, and Russian forces destroyed some of them themselves because of poor coordination between units.
Gubarev put the price of a single Lancet at 3 million to 5.5 million rubles ($37,000 to $67,000), meaning the unit spent roughly 300 million to 500 million rubles (about $3.7 million to $6.1 million) on the three hits. The Oryx open-source project has estimated the cost of a Lancet at about $35,000, in line with his figures.
He blamed the unit’s leadership rather than its operators, saying commanders used the expensive drones without proper preparation while sending reports of supposedly successful results up the chain of command.
“There are no questions about the technical side of the UAV launches: the fighters did their job conscientiously and properly. The questions are for the commanders,” said Pavel Gubarev.
Gubarev, who declared himself “people’s governor” of Donetsk during Russia’s 2014 seizure of parts of eastern Ukraine, regularly comments on the Russian war effort on social media.
The Lancet is a family of loitering munitions built by ZALA Aero, part of Russia’s Kalashnikov Group. The drone has two sets of X-shaped wings mounted along a composite fuselage, with an optical seeker in the nose, the warhead, battery and electric motor in the middle, and a pusher propeller at the tail. Crews launch it from a catapult and fly it from a briefcase-style control station.
The stated range is more than 40 km (25 miles), and estimates based on the distances to targets it has struck suggest a maximum range of about 50 km (31 miles). Some versions carry a KZ-6 shaped-charge warhead weighing about 3 kg (6.6 pounds), which, according to available descriptions, is fixed inside the fuselage with mounting foam even though the charge was not designed to be used that way.
For much of the war, the Lancet was among Russia’s most effective weapons against Ukrainian artillery and armored vehicles. Ukrainian forces have since shot down growing numbers of the drones, including with interceptor drones that hunt them in the air.

articles.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine kill four and injure 28, authorities say
articles.body:
Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russia has launched roughly 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones against Ukraine over the past week.
Russian strikes on Ukraine's eastern Dnipro region on Saturday night left four people dead and 22 injured, authorities have announced, with a separate attack on Vinnytsia in west-central Ukraine injuring another six people.
Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, said Russian forces had targeted the Dnipro area with drones and aerial bombs, striking three districts more than 20 times.
The attacks damaged infrastructure in Dnipro city and destroyed private homes, apartment buildings, stores and cars in the Synelnykivskyi district, he said. A private home was also damaged in the Nikopol district, he added.
In a post on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian drone had also hit a high-rise apartment building in Vinnytsia, while a hypermarket had been targeted in Kharkiv in the northeast of the country.
"In Kharkiv, the Russians first struck a home improvement hypermarket and then carried out a cynical double-tap strike on the emergency services that arrived at the scene," he wrote, adding that an unspecified number of emergency responders had been injured.
The Ukrainian leader also reported overnight strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities, including a thermal power plant and substations.
According to Zelenskyy, Russia has launched roughly 1,600 guided aerial bombs, 48 missiles and nearly 2,300 attack drones against Ukraine over the past week.
Ukrainian forces hit back on Saturday and overnight with their own strikes against Russian targets, including army radar stations, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
Ukraine's military also struck command posts as well as Russian "personnel concentrations," per the General Staff.
"Striking radars creates gaps in the enemy’s radar coverage and expands the Defence Forces of Ukraine’s ability to employ unmanned systems at all levels," it said.
Starlink access restored
It comes after Kyiv announced on Saturday that its forces had re-established a "stable" connection to Elon Musk's Starlink network amid a dispute with the US.
"The speeds are now where they need to be. The restoration began overnight, and by this morning, speeds were already sufficient," Zelenskyy said. "This matters: for our frontline logistics, for defending Ukraine against jet-powered 'shaheds.'"
Starlink, and its military version Starshield, have proved crucial to the Ukrainian military's operations as it has continued to battle Russian President Vladimir Putin's invading forces, providing resilient internet and communications over the battlefield.

articles.title: News from occupied Ukraine: Former Oleshky resident warns people 'won't survive this winter'
articles.body:
News from occupied Ukraine: Former Oleshky resident warns people 'won't survive this winter'
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Key news as of Oct. 25:
- Oleshky native warns residents may not survive winter as evacuation hopes rise
- Russian-occupied Crimea imposes power and water restrictions after drone attack
- Russia sentences 77-year-old Crimean activist to 18 years over alleged plot against Moscow's proxy
- At least 34 Ukrainians were brought back from occupied territories, including over 20 children
- Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says
- Data center in occupied Donetsk destroyed following Ukraine's strikes
A woman who fled Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has warned that residents remaining in the town may not survive the winter, as hopes grow for a possible evacuation mission.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
"If the evacuation goes ahead, it will be a lifeline for those who remain. People won't survive the winter," a woman who left Oleshky in recent months told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 24. She declined to reveal her name for security reasons.
The woman pointed to severe food shortages and a lack of fuel for heating and cooking. She said residents had already burned much of the available wood during the previous winter, leaving few options to keep their homes warm as temperatures fall.
"There is almost no chance of survival," she added.
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around Oleshky to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on Oct. 23.
Under the agreement, a ceasefire will be implemented, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky, and civilians will be allowed to leave the city freely, according to Lubinets.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 24 that Ukraine will fulfill its part of the "extremely difficult" humanitarian operation in Oleshky.
The move came amid increased attention to the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city, which over the past weeks has gained international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV.
Despite hoping the evacuation would proceed, the woman expressed concern that Russian authorities could prevent it from going ahead.
"I'd like to believe that this mission will go ahead, but you can expect anything from the Russian Federation," she said, adding that she believed civilians were being kept in the area as human shields.
Stefan Vorontsov, a volunteer coordinator with the NGO Humanity, which helps evacuate civilians from occupied territories, told the Kyiv Independent that while he hoped that people would be saved, he expects Russian provocations, blackmail, and propaganda surrounding those who manage to get out.
"God willing, we will be able to set a precedent where Russia admits what they did in the occupied territories, and we will be able to organize the first official evacuation from there, then maybe the rest of us will be able to do it too. But again, I have little faith," Vorontsov said.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help Oleshky residents leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. Now, they said, the risk of Russian attacks and mines has made organized evacuation impossible.
In recent months, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces. At the end of September, four people were attempting to leave the town when they stepped on a mine and were injured, while a man collecting nuts was killed by another mine.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town with severely limited access to food, drinking water, electricity, and other basic services.
