Russian-occupied Crimea imposes power and water restrictions after drone attack
Russian-installed authorities in occupied Crimea introduced electricity and water restrictions on Oct. 24 following a reported Ukrainian drone attack on energy infrastructure outside the peninsula, the Russian proxy governor of occupied Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said.
The restrictions came after Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Russia on Oct. 23-24, including damage to the Taman substation in Krasnodar Krai, which supplies electricity to occupied Crimea.
Major cities, including Sevastopol and Yalta, were left without electricity following the hit on the key power station.
Aksyonov said repairs were underway while rolling power cuts were implemented.
In Sevastopol, Russian-installed governor Mikhail Razvozhaev said on Oct. 25 that renewed strain on the power grid had prompted rolling blackouts on a "three hours on, three hours off" schedule.
Razvozhaev added that electricity supply to industrial sites and shopping centers will be restricted "as much as possible" to reduce the load on the grid.
"The capacity freed up must be channeled first and foremost to residential properties. This is our top priority," Razvozhaev said.
Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on the evening of Oct. 23 that "the entire peninsula" was without electricity.
Crimea, which was occupied and illegally annexed by Russian forces in 2014, has been hit with widespread power outages before. This summer, Ukrainian forces reportedly hit 16 power stations across Crimea in 48 hours, in an effort to hinder Moscow in its war effort.

Russia sentences 77-year-old Crimean activist to 18 years over alleged plot against Moscow's proxy
A Russian court in Rostov-on-Don said on Oct. 22 it had sentenced 77-year-old Crimean political prisoner Volodymyr Ananiev to 18 years in prison over an alleged plot to assassinate Sergey Aksyonov, the Russian proxy governor.
"Volodymyr Ananiev is the oldest Crimean political prisoner. He suffers from vision problems and issues with his spine, muscles, kidneys, and legs, and walks with a cane," The NGO Crimean Tatar Resource Center said.
Ananiev was detained in the Russian-occupied city of Simferopol in February 2024. Russian investigators claimed Ananiev was part of a group that tracked Aksyonov's car and prepared an explosive device to blow it up.
Moscow has continued to repress Crimean Tatars and other residents, including journalists and activists, of the peninsula since its occupation in 2014. Around 300 people, including journalists and activists, were being held on politically motivated charges as of spring, more than 150 of them Crimean Tatars, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said.

At least 34 Ukrainians brought back from occupied territories, including over 20 children
Over the past week, Ukraine brought back at least 34 citizens who were forced to stay in Russian-occupied territories, including 23 children, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA said.
On Oct. 22, Lubinets said that 11 Ukrainian citizens returned to government-controlled territory. Some of those who returned faced additional challenges due to health conditions, the need for medical care, and difficulties arranging a safe way back.
Among them was a married couple whose return journey involved two attempts. The woman had previously managed to leave occupied territory, but returned after her husband became seriously ill and was admitted to intensive care. After his condition improved, she arranged for them to leave together.
Separately, Bring Kids Back UA announced on Oct. 19 that it brought home 23 more children from Russian-occupied territory.
Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory was 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, including instruction in handling grenades and firearms, the statement said.
The Ukrainian ombudsman's office coordinates returns through the humanitarian route connecting Mokrany in Belarus with Domanove in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast. Lubinets said the office is effectively the only Ukrainian state institution systematically organizing returns from occupied territories through this route, assisting people who cannot leave independently.
The Volyn humanitarian corridor is the main working checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus. There are currently no functioning checkpoints between Ukraine and Russia.
According to Lubinets, 24,953 people, including 2,054 children, returned to Ukraine through this humanitarian corridor between May 24, 2024, and Oct. 15, 2026. Of these, 11,815 people, including 802 children, returned in 2026 alone.

Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says
Russian security forces carried out a new round of raids across occupied Ukrainian territories in early October, targeting residents who have refused to obtain Russian passports, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said on Oct. 22.
The raids were conducted jointly by the Russian police and the Federal Security Service (FSB) during the first 10 days of October as part of an operation dubbed "Illegal-2026," according to HUR.
Ukrainians without Russian passports are classified by occupation authorities as "foreign citizens" and subjected to Russian migration law.
According to the agency, residents can face pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, expulsion from occupied territory, dismissal from work, and property seizure.
Russia has pressured residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to take Russian passports since 2014, tying access to employment, social services, property rights, and other aspects of daily life to possession of Russian documents.
This is part of Moscow's long-running campaign of forced passportization. Russian President Vladimir Putin, on March 4, signed a decree that indefinitely extended the simplified process of obtaining Russian citizenship in the occupied territories.
"The goal of the decree is to passportize as many people as possible, pressuring them," Nataliia Yurlova, lawyer for the NGO Donbas SOS, told the Kyiv Independent.

Ukraine's reported attack on a building in the occupied city of Donetsk, Donetsk Oblast, destroyed a data center on Oct. 20, according to Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation.
Andriushchenko told the Kyiv Independent that a data center used by Ugletelecom and Elecom, a major telecom operator in occupied Donetsk Oblast, was hit at Postysheva St. 60, according to his sources.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that explosions were heard in Donetsk this morning and shared footage showing the damaged facade of the building on Postysheva St. 60.
The head of Russia's proxies in the city of Donetsk, Alexey Kulemzin, reported a Ukrainian attack on the city and shared video footage of the same damaged building on Telegram.
Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted each other’s data centers after a Russian attack damaged a Kyiv data center housing network equipment for internet provider UTELS, causing service disruptions on Sept. 23.

articles.title: Pope’s envoy becomes first foreign representative to gain access to Ukrainian POWs held by Russia since 2022
articles.body:
Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said a foreign representative was allowed to physically visit Ukrainian prisoners of war held by Russia for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.
The visit by Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, Pope Leo XIV’s special envoy, marks a potential step toward greater access to Ukrainian captives, whom Russia has largely kept inaccessible to international humanitarian organizations.
Cardinal Zuppi visits Ukrainian POWs
Lubinets said he had been informed that Zuppi was allowed to meet Ukrainian servicemembers held in Russian captivity. The prisoners also confirmed that representatives of Russia’s human rights ombudsman had begun visiting them.
Lubinets said he regularly meets with Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova. At their latest meeting, the two discussed further steps toward returning Ukrainian citizens held by Russia.
“Every exchange is negotiations,” Lubinets said, adding that each one offers a chance to make progress on returning both prisoners of war and civilians.
During his three-day Moscow visit in September, Zuppi also met with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, Russia’s human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova, and children’s rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova, according to Vatican News.
The discussions covered missing persons, family reunification, and the return of Ukrainian children, with Zuppi calling for faster checks to help families reunite.
Lubinets said he hoped the new access would continue and pledged to keep working toward the return of all Ukrainian citizens held in Russian places of detention.
Russia blocks access to Ukrainian captives
Russia has kept the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) from accessing Ukrainian prisoners of war since 2024. The ICRC is mandated under the Geneva Conventions to visit prisoners of war and monitor their treatment.
Around 1,500 Ukrainians held by Russia have never had their status as prisoners confirmed by the ICRC and face prosecution, according to Ukraine. Without confirmation of their captivity, their families may lack official acknowledgment of their whereabouts and status.
Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution
On 23 October, Ukraine returned 270 people from Russian captivity, including 261 military personnel and nine civilians. The released captives included five survivors of Russia’s July 2022 attack on the Olenivka prison barracks, as well as Ukrainian defenders held since 2018.

articles.title: Houthis claim 7 attacks on Saudi targets as heavy airstrikes hit Yemen
articles.body:
SANAA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Saturday that it had launched seven missile and drone attacks on airports, oil facilities and a military base across Saudi Arabia, as heavy Saudi-led airstrikes hit various Houthi-held areas of Yemen.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a statement broadcast by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV that the group had used ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting airports, oil facilities and a military base in the Saudi cities of Riyadh, Yanbu, Rabigh, Dammam, Najran and Khamis Mushait.
Sarea said King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was targeted in two stages. Other attacks struck targets including Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the claimed strikes.
Sarea said the attacks were launched after what he described as 100 Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-held areas of Yemen over the previous 24 hours. He claimed Saudi Arabia had carried out a total of 3,123 air and missile strikes on Yemen since the latest escalation began.
Meanwhile, al-Masirah TV reported on Saturday casualties from heavy Saudi-led airstrikes across Houthi-held areas. It said four people were killed and several others wounded when a house was hit in the Asr neighborhood of the capital Sanaa, citing a preliminary toll.
In the western province of Hodeidah, five members of one family were killed when an airstrike hit their home in the At Tuhayta district, while another child was wounded, according to al-Masirah.
The broadcaster also reported that eight people were killed and more than 10 others wounded in airstrikes on housing for cement factory workers in Hamdan district of Sanaa province.
Separately, Sarea said in a statement posted on social media platform X that Houthi forces had targeted what he called Saudi-backed "mobilizations" at Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in the southern port city of Aden, where Yemen's internationally recognized government is based.
The strikes came amid an intensifying confrontation between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition, with missile, drone and air attacks escalating across several parts of the country in recent days.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: Russian titanium plant in Urals reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones, 1,500 km from Ukraine

A drone attack damaged an industrial facility in Russia’s Perm Krai early on 25 October, injuring five workers, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported. Exilenova+ identified the target as the AVISMA chemical and metallurgical plant in Berezniki, around 1,500 km from Ukraine’s border.
The reported strike highlights Ukraine’s ability to reach industrial facilities deep inside Russia that support its military-industrial complex.
AVISMA produces titanium materials used in aviation and aerospace manufacturing, including military aircraft, aircraft engines, missiles, and space technology, according to Exilenova+.
Regional governor Dmitry Makhonin said the industrial facility sustained damage but continued operating normally. He said five workers were injured in the attack.
A target deep inside Russia
Perm Krai lies in Russia’s Ural region, roughly 1,500 km from Ukraine’s border. The distance places the reported strike far beyond Russia’s border regions, where Ukrainian drone attacks have frequently targeted military and industrial infrastructure.
The reported attack follows a broader Ukrainian campaign against Russian industrial and energy facilities linked to the country’s war effort.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that air defenses intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian drones overnight across 23 Russian regions and over the Sea of Azov, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
The reported interceptions included drones over Perm Krai, as well as regions around Moscow and areas in southern and western Russia. The figures have not been independently verified.
The extent of damage at AVISMA and any impact on its operations have not been independently established.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts 10 Houthi ballistic missiles targeting southern Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Sunday that it intercepted and destroyed 10 ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi group from Yemen toward Saudi Arabia’s southern region, Anadolu reports.
Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said on US social media company X that the missiles were shot down, without giving any details about injuries or damage.
His announcement came after he said earlier in the day that the coalition intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile that targeted the southwestern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.
Maliki also said that coalition forces had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile and two drones launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh.
The developments came amid escalating hostilities involving attacks on Saudi aviation and energy infrastructure and coalition strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis since 2015.

articles.title: Houthis fire missiles at Saudi Arabia as Riyadh airport reopens
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis fire missiles at Saudi Arabia as Riyadh airport reopens
Yemen's Houthis launched wide-ranging strikes across swathes of southern Saudi Arabia on Sunday, as the kingdom announced the partial reopening of Riyadh's international airport despite repeated attacks by the group.
Alerts warning of possible attacks were activated across the kingdom's south throughout the day, with the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis saying at least 10 ballistic missiles were intercepted.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart.
"The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning - may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions," one resident in Khamis Mushait told AFP Sunday on condition of anonymity.
Further north, Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes.
However it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.
The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target".
"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines - as well as staff and travellers - against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.
"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."
Attack warning
As the airport prepared to open, AFP journalists in Riyadh heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards the capital, as well as two drones in the capital area.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.
Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city along with areas in Taif, Namas and Jazan.
The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that - in the space of 24 hours - they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.
The Saudi civil defence agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a "huge lie".
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets.
The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image.

articles.title: British and French troops war-game attack on NATO territory
articles.body:
British and French troops war-game attack on NATO territory

- About 2,500 troops took part over seven weeks, with 600 paratroopers dropping from four RAF A400M Atlas aircraft in one of Britain’s largest airborne operations in 20 years.
- The drill comes amid fears of Russian aggression in Europe, and Wes Streeting said it shows NATO can deliver rapid airborne power to defend territory and deter adversaries.

LONDON – Thousands of British and French troops have taken part in a military training exercise that included one of Britain’s largest airborne operations in two decades, the British government said on Oct 25.
The war game is designed to show how NATO countries could be defended against a modern-day attack and comes during fears about Russian aggression in Europe amid Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Some 2,500 troops were involved in the seven-week exercise, in which 600 British and French paratroopers dropped from four RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft over Germany.
The exercise, called Rhino Titan and held at the Sennelager military training centre in Germany, has been testing British troops’ ability against an enemy equipped with drones and electronic warfare.
“The threats we face in the 21st century require an updated, modern approach to warfare – and our adaptable armed forces are preparing accordingly,” British Defence Minister Wes Streeting said in a statement.
“Alongside our French and German allies, this large-scale training exercise shows we can deliver rapid, large-scale airborne power anywhere it’s needed to defend NATO territory.
“This combination of troops and specialised equipment is what is required to deter adversaries and keep Britain and our allies safe,” he added.

However, Trump conceded that direct trade measures would likely have minimal impact due to limited bilateral trade volumes.
“We ended five wars thanks to tariffs. I said, ‘If you continue to fight, we’re going to put a 200 percent tariff on you,’ and they stopped,” Trump told supporters in Florida.
“We should probably immediately do it with Ukraine and Russia. Never thought of it. But we don’t buy enough to do it to them, so it doesn’t work.”
‘Trump Is Cooked’: Republicans Clash Over Ukraine as Midterms Loom
The administration has increasingly utilized trade restrictions, tariff waivers, and commercial agreements as central instruments in its diplomatic maneuvering ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections.
Disputed economic leverage
Trump’s focus on future commercial engagement with Moscow and Kyiv unfolds amid continuing friction regarding Washington’s economic tools to influence the conflict.
President Volodymyr Zelensky previously stated that the US president possesses statutory leverage to compel Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate, emphasizing that bipartisan sanctions approved by the US Congress remain unenacted at the White House.
“Trump could very easily bring Putin to the negotiating table, because he has the means to do so. The way he speaks about me – President Trump should speak about Putin in the same way,” Zelensky said.
“Sanctions are sitting on his desk. He didn’t vote for them – Congress voted for strong sanctions. He has the power to act.”
Ukraine’s head of state also rejected assertions by the Trump administration linking retail fuel price increases in the United States to Ukrainian long-range drone interdiction strikes on Russian oil refineries.
While Trump justified a bilateral commercial arrangement to facilitate Russian diesel sales on global markets to lower consumer costs, Zelensky stated that domestic US diesel benchmarks operate independently of Russian export volumes.
Sanctions waivers
The debate over commercial relations arrives after Trump’s recent decision to suspend statutory sanctions and trade duties codified under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
On Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Graham Act to waive mandatory 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent secondary duties targeting global buyers of Russian hydrocarbons, just 48 hours before the measures were scheduled to take statutory effect.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the suspension as a 60-day pause to assess the broader economic fallout of tariffs on both the US and international economies, citing third-party dependencies such as India’s reliance on Russian crude.

articles.title: Netanyahu posts image of atomic bomb over Tel Aviv: ‘Nothing else will matter’
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday shared an AI-generated image depicting an atomic bomb falling on Tel Aviv, accompanied by a stark warning about Iran's nuclear ambitions, just two days before Israelis head to the polls. The post, which suggested that domestic political controversies pale in comparison with the threat from Tehran, drew a sharp response from Democrats party chairman Yair Golan, who accused Netanyahu of spreading panic.
Alongside the image, Netanyahu quoted Yuval Bloomberg, an Israeli writer and political commentator best known for his book The Oslo Trap, which critically examines the 1993 Oslo Accords and their consequences for Israeli security.
"The State of Israel faces a real and tangible existential threat," Bloomberg wrote. "If the Iranians obtain nuclear weapons, nothing else will matter anymore. Everything is so trivial compared with the existential danger posed by Iran and the Shiite axis."
The post also repeated the argument that Israel has only two more years under U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to address the Iranian threat, portraying disputes dominating Israeli politics as distractions from the country's most pressing security challenge.
"Qatar, the ultra-Orthodox, Urich, military conscription, warnings. It's all one giant smokescreen designed to conceal the one issue that towers above everything else," the post read. "If two atomic bombs fall on central Israel, who will care about all these meaningless controversies?"
The image and accompanying message came as Israel entered the final stretch of its election campaign, with voters set to cast their ballots Tuesday, October 27. Netanyahu has emphasized the threat from Iran throughout the campaign, arguing that confronting Tehran's nuclear ambitions must remain Israel's overriding national priority.
Golan, a former IDF deputy chief of staff and chairman of the Democrats party, condemned the post and accused the prime minister of attempting to frighten voters.
"The prime minister of Israel has posted an image of an atomic bomb falling on Tel Aviv," Golan said. "I ask that he be kept away from social media. The man and those around him have lost it. The pressure is mounting."
Golan also linked his criticism directly to the upcoming election, saying: "On Tuesday, we will replace those spreading panic and restore security and sanity to Israel."

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Musk of false claims over Starlink
articles.body:
- Ukraine rejected Elon Musk’s claim that its military used civilian Starlink for offensive drone strikes in breach of SpaceX’s terms of service.
- Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Starlink terminals in Ukraine have been capped at 70-90 km/h since February 2026 and do not work over Russia.
Ukraine has rejected Elon Musk’s claim that its military broke Starlink’s terms of service by using the civilian satellite network for offensive drone strikes, with a presidential adviser saying that restrictions SpaceX placed on the service in February make such use physically impossible.
Musk made the accusation on X on Oct. 24, the same day Ukraine said its satellite access had been restored after more than a week of speed restrictions that disrupted front-line operations.
“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” wrote SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
In the same post, Musk said Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade version of the network, “is controlled by the US government,” and that Starlink remains critical to Ukraine’s defense because it is “the only system that cannot be jammed or blown up, at least for now.” He wrote that Ukraine’s front line “would collapse immediately” if Starlink were turned off, said SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth, and closed by telling people he called warmongers, “May you burn in hell.”
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technology, responded that Musk’s claim ignores how Starlink actually works in Ukraine. Since February 2026, he said, every Starlink terminal over Ukrainian territory, including occupied areas, has been capped at movement speeds of 70 to 90 km/h (43 to 56 mph), and Starlink does not work over Russia at all.
“It is very strange that Elon Musk does not know about the restrictions on Starlink’s operation in Ukraine,” said Beskrestnov. “Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and middle strikes.”
A terminal capped at road speeds cannot stay connected aboard an attack drone, and the long-range strikes Musk referred to take place over Russian territory, where the service is switched off.
Serhii Sternenko, who worked on the issue at Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense as an adviser to Mykhailo Fedorov, said the system Ukraine built in February left no room for the misuse Musk described. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians, but any terminal used on the move had to be placed on a special list and connected to Starshield.
“In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield,” wrote Sternenko.
“We are very grateful to the United States and SpaceX for access to critically important satellite communications. Ukraine did not violate the terms of use,” wrote Sternenko.
Musk’s Oct. 24 post differs from what he said 10 days earlier. On Oct. 14, as speed limits disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, Mykhailo Fedorov wrote on X that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h (99 mph) was being restored and that removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely had become critical for Ukraine’s defense. Musk replied the same day that the limits were not SpaceX’s decision.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” wrote Musk on Oct. 14. “Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
President Donald Trump has said he did not order the restrictions. CBS News and The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week that Musk was behind the slowdown, and his Oct. 24 post was the first time he said SpaceX had closed what he called a loophole.
Ukrainian commanders said the restrictions cost them drones and disrupted missions. Starshield has become the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and battlefield communications, including the interceptor drones used against Russian attack drones. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said on Oct. 24 that full use had been restored, with its monitoring systems recording stable connections on objects moving faster than 400 km/h (250 mph).

articles.title: Houthis renew strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities
articles.body:
Houthis renew strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities
Yemen’s Houthis have struck several targets in Saudi Arabia, including two international airports and energy infrastructure facilities operated by the oil giant Saudi Aramco, the group’s military spokesman said on Saturday.
The conflict between Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, also known as the Houthis, and the Saudi-led coalition escalated last month, when the militant group seized the Red Sea port cities of Mocha and Dhubab as well as Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have since tightened their siege of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city and a key stronghold of anti-Houthi forces.
In a statement posted on X, Yahya Saree said the Houthis had conducted seven operations using ballistic missiles and drones, targeting King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran Airport and Khamis Mushait Air Base, as well as Aramco’s facilities in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery and crude oil pumping stations, and a pipeline linking eastern and western Saudi Arabia.
The spokesman said the attacks were carried out in response to what the group described as Saudi “aggression” against Yemen. Saree claimed Saudi forces had launched 100 airstrikes over the previous 24 hours, targeting civilian infrastructure in Sanaa and other areas, leaving dozens dead and wounded. 
He said the Houthis would continue attacking Saudi territory until the “aggression” ends and the Saudi-led coalition lifts its restrictions on the movement of goods and people into and out of Yemen.
The latest attack came as Riyadh’s main air hub prepared to resume operations after more than two weeks of disruption following earlier Houthi strikes. The facility announced a partial reopening from Sunday. In a separate post on X, Saree warned that airlines, airport staff and passengers against using the site, calling it a military target and saying it would remain unsafe.
The spokesman also accused Riyadh of spreading false claims that the Houthis had targeted the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, insisting that the group’s operations were directed solely at Saudi oil facilities and military bases and were announced as they took place.
The accusation came in response to Saudi Civil Defense claims that debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis fell in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday. The debris landed in several locations, including Wadi Al-Mughammas in Mecca, Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh, the agency said on Saturday.
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, with Saudi Arabia leading a military intervention the following year to support the internationally recognized government against the Houthis. Fighting eased under a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but escalated sharply in September 2026.
The renewed conflict has seen the Houthis launch missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, while the Riyadh-led coalition has intensified airstrikes on Houthi positions, command centers and weapons networks.
The Houthis have claimed the total number of Saudi airstrikes and missile attacks since the latest escalation began has reached 3,123.

articles.body:
Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles and drones as fighting with Houthis rages
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted drone and missile launched towards Riyadh and 10 missiles targeting the southern region.
Saudi Arabia has intercepted drones and missiles over its capital, Riyadh, and southern areas, the Saudi-led coalition has said, as fighting with Yemen’s Houthis continues.
Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said on Sunday its forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the capital city that morning, as well as a drone in the Riyadh region, and a cruise missile aimed at the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, with explosions ringing out in the Saudi capital.
It later reported the interception of 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.
The fall of debris following the destruction of two ballistic missiles in Khamis Mushait and Ahad Rafidah caused two injuries, the Saudi Civil Defence agency said. In a post on X, it added the shrapnel also damaged three residential buildings and seven vehicles.
The attacks come as operations resumed at two terminals at Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid international airport after deadly attacks earlier this month by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
Operations at the airport were halted on October 10 after 13 people were killed and more than 300 others were wounded in a Houthi attack.
Late on Saturday, Riyadh airport said in a statement that international flights would resume from Terminal 2 on Sunday, while Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target” for the Iran-backed group.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travellers – against using King Khalid airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces,” he said. “The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport.”
The Iran-aligned Houthis on Saturday said they targeted three Saudi airports, including one in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an airbase.
The Saudi civil defence agency said it also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting Mecca and Medina, two of the holiest cities in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a “huge lie”.
In Yemen on Sunday, the Houthis advanced on Jabal Sabr, the strategic mountain overlooking the city of Taiz, which has become the focus of the fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s government forces.
Houthi fighters have besieged the city and cut off the main road to Aden, which serves as the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The United Nations has warned that “time is running out” to deliver aid to the 800,000 people trapped in the city.
Yemen’s government forces, meanwhile, said they conducted more than 700 operations against Houthi targets on Saturday, claiming to have killed more than 300 fighters.
Fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters has intensified across multiple fronts in Yemen in recent weeks, causing a spiralling humanitarian crisis.
The war in Yemen escalated sharply when the Houthis seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, which is aligned with Yemen’s government forces, have dealt a huge blow to the kingdom, the world’s biggest exporter of crude oil, disrupting its businesses, airlines and normal life, and damaging its international image.

China Flexes Its Naval Muscles Near Japan With Ukraine-Built Aircraft Carrier
China has deployed its first aircraft carrier, Liaoning, originally built at a shipyard in Ukraine, to waters near Japan as part of a major naval training operation in the Western Pacific, prompting Japanese fighter jets to scramble in response to Chinese carrier-based aviation activity.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The deployment marks another milestone in the transformation of the former Soviet aircraft carrier Varyag, constructed in Mykolaiv, Ukraine, from an unfinished Cold War-era warship into a centerpiece of China’s growing naval power.
According to Defence Blog on October 24, citing Chinese state broadcaster CCTV and Japan’s Joint Staff, the Liaoning carrier group completed its second Western Pacific training deployment of 2026, a decade after its first such voyage in 2016.
Japanese forces initially detected the carrier on October 13, accompanied by two Renhai-class destroyers, hull numbers 103 and 104, and a Luyang III-class destroyer, hull number 123.
The following day, the Chinese naval group sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako-jima into the Pacific Ocean. Japanese maritime forces subsequently observed fighter aircraft taking off and landing aboard Liaoning approximately 250 kilometers (155 miles) south of Ishigaki Island.
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets in response to the Chinese aircraft activity, according to the Japanese Joint Staff. By October 15, all four Chinese vessels had been observed heading toward the South China Sea.
Liaoning’s origins trace back to Ukraine’s major shipbuilding industry. Originally named Varyag, the Soviet-era aircraft carrier was constructed at the Black Sea Shipyard in the Ukrainian city of Mykolaiv, one of the Soviet Union’s most important naval shipbuilding centers.
Following Ukraine’s independence in 1991, the unfinished carrier came under Ukrainian ownership before being sold to Chinese buyers. Beijing subsequently completed and modernized the vessel, commissioning it into its navy as Liaoning in 2012.
The Ukrainian-built hull became the foundation of China’s first aircraft carrier, helping Beijing establish its own carrier program. According to Chinese military commentator Du Wenlong, the reconstruction process allowed Chinese engineers to acquire essential aircraft carrier design and construction expertise.
Over the following decade, Liaoning evolved from a training platform into a combat-capable warship and flagship of its carrier group, equipped with upgraded weapons, aviation, and command systems.
Earlier, China deployed naval and air forces near the disputed Scarborough Shoal in the South China Sea as the US, the Philippines, and regional allies conducted major joint military exercises. The coordinated wave against Epicentr centers coincided with broader strikes on commercial and municipal logistics, including the overnight destruction of an emergency fire-tanker truck in Kharkiv during secondary strikes on first responders and an attack on a warehouse in Lozova that killed a 45-year-old commercial employee.
Pattern of commercial retail interdiction
Ukrainian municipal authorities and retail operators have repeatedly emphasized that systematic standoff strikes directed against large-scale construction hypermarkets, civilian shopping hubs, and logistics warehouses serve no military objective.
Epicentr hypermarkets function as primary commercial centers for building supplies, consumer goods, and municipal repair materials utilized by local populations and utility services to restore homes and infrastructure following aerial bombardments.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine report deaths and injuries in overnight strikes
articles.body:
At least three people were killed and 16 injured in Ukrainian attacks on Russia, while 10 people were injured in Russian strikes on Ukraine, officials from both countries said on Sunday.
In Russia, two people were killed and two seriously injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on a minibus belonging to an agricultural enterprise in the village of Borshchovo in the Bryansk region, regional head Yegor Kovalchuk said.
In Belgorod, one person was killed and 14 injured in a large-scale overnight drone attack, regional Governor Alexander Shuvaev said on the Russian social media platform Max.
In Ukraine, 10 people, including three emergency responders, were injured in Russian strikes in Kharkiv and Vinnytsia, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
Six more people were injured in a Russian strike on a residential five-story building in Vinnytsia, it added.
The attacks sparked fires, and emergency crews came under repeated strikes while responding to the incidents, the service said.
A fire engine tanker was completely destroyed, it added.
Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces continued overnight strikes against logistics centers, port infrastructure facilities in Ukraine and vessels allegedly carrying supplies for Ukrainian forces.
In Kharkiv, Russian strikes hit the Epicentr logistics center, a distribution center and the Vasyshchevo logistics terminal, it said.
According to the ministry, the facilities were used to store military or dual-use goods intended to support Ukraine's armed forces.
The ministry also claimed that a dry cargo vessel carrying supplies for Ukrainian forces was struck while crossing the sea en route to the port of Chornomorsk.
Russian air defences intercepted and destroyed 532 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over 25 Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.
The claims from both sides could not be independently verified.

articles.title: Russia Transferred Over $80 Million in Submarine Technology to China
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Transferred Over $80 Million in Submarine Technology to China
Russia supplied China with more than $80 million worth of submarine-related technology and technical documentation, helping Beijing develop its conventional submarine fleet through cooperation that continued after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to an October 22 report titled A Marriage of Convenience? by the Washington-based research organization C4ADS, Russia’s Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering conducted 12 shipments to Chinese military procurement agencies and China Shipbuilding and Offshore International Co. (CSOI) between August 2015 and April 2023.
The transfers, valued at more than $80 million, reportedly involved conceptual designs for non-nuclear submarines, testing documentation, and technologies intended to improve underwater stealth.
Two shipments in October 2019 and January 2020 included documents related to submarine testing, particularly cavitation—a phenomenon that generates underwater noise and can make submarines easier to detect.
A maritime security expert consulted by C4ADS assessed that the documentation indicated Russian assistance in evaluating Chinese submarine noise-reduction technologies.
The cooperation also operated in the opposite direction. Between December 2019 and September 2022, CSOI supplied Rubin with submarine testing equipment, including instruments and control-panel components used to evaluate onboard information and control systems.
Documents accompanying a September 2022 shipment also referenced a joint design and manufacturing contract, indicating that technical cooperation continued after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Rubin, a subsidiary of Russia’s state-owned United Shipbuilding Corporation, is subject to sanctions imposed by the United States, European Union, and Japan.
China’s conventional submarine fleet has historically relied on Soviet and Russian technology, although Beijing has since developed its own designs. The C4ADS findings indicate that Russian expertise continued to support Chinese submarine development, particularly in acoustic stealth and underwater systems.
Earlier, an October 19 report revealed that Chinese companies had supplied Russia with industrial equipment, engine components, and navigation technology, helping expand production of Shahed-type attack drones at the Alabuga facility to a reported capacity of more than 3,000 per month.

articles.title: Could Hormuz become America’s Suez?
articles.body:
In 1956, Britain was forced to abandon the Suez Canal and withdraw from Egypt after a humiliating political and financial defeat. The crisis did not end the British Empire overnight, but it exposed the decline of a power that had dominated much of the world for more than two centuries, in an empire on which the sun famously never set. Britain could still fight wars, but it could no longer act as an independent global power without facing the economic and political limits of its strength. Now, nearly seventy years later, the question is whether the war with Iran and the crisis around the Strait of Hormuz could become America’s Suez.
When war becomes too expensive
After Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in July 1956, Britain, France and Israel launched a military campaign to regain control of the canal and weaken Nasser’s government. Their forces made rapid progress, but the operation soon became a financial and political crisis for London.
The British pound came under heavy pressure, and the Bank of England had to use its dollar reserves to defend the currency. The United States opposed the invasion and refused to provide the financial support Britain needed unless it agreed to stop the operation. On 6th November, Britain accepted a ceasefire. It later withdrew its forces from Egypt.
As the International Monetary Fund’s account of the crisis explains, the pressure on sterling was central to Britain’s decision. The crisis showed that the government could not continue the war without putting its financial position at long-term risk.
The war with Iran could create a similar problem for the United States, although the economic conditions are different. The dollar is far stronger internationally than the pound was in 1956, and the American economy has greater resources. But the comparison is about the cost of sustaining a war when its political goals remain out of reach.
If the war continues without a clear result, the United States will have to spend more on military operations, weapons, logistics and the protection of its forces. At the same time, the disruption of energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz can raise costs across the global economy. These pressures may gradually make the war harder to justify, especially if Iran can draw the United States into a prolonged conflict with no clear progress toward its goals.
The cost reaches American households
The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem because of its role in the global energy market. Before the war, around one-fifth of the world’s oil consumption passed through the strait, along with a major share of global liquefied natural gas shipments. As oil prices rose, gasoline and diesel became more expensive, air travel and shipping costs increased, and the cost of transporting goods went up. This is where the war became a serious domestic problem for the White House. Higher gasoline prices were immediately visible to American households. Families had to spend more to drive for daily activities and higher diesel prices increased the cost of moving goods.
The latest energy-market reports show how difficult this problem can even become. In October 2026, Reuters reported that Brent crude remained above $100 a barrel. Diesel prices in the United States had also risen sharply, adding to domestic political pressure ahead of the midterm elections. The Reuters report on rising oil prices and the prolonged conflict describes the growing challenge for the Trump administration.
High energy prices can also make it harder to control inflation. Transport and production become more expensive, and the effects spread through the economy. If the Federal Reserve keeps interest rates high to control inflation, borrowing becomes more expensive for households and businesses. The government also has to meet the direct cost of the war while paying interest on its existing debt.
Nevertheless, none of these pressures would force Washington to end the war. The key issue is their combined effect over time. If the war continues, energy prices remain high and the United States fails to achieve objectives, the economic cost of continuing may eventually become greater than the expected benefit.
From military leverage to economic limits
A war of attrition changes the way governments calculate success. At the beginning of a conflict, leaders may expect military action to produce a quick political result. If that result does not come, they face a difficult choice: increase the pressure and spend more, or accept that the original goals may be impossible to achieve at an acceptable cost.
This is the danger facing the United States. Washington has the ability to strike Iranian targets and maintain a strong military presence in the region. But the ability to damage does not mean that Iran will accept American demands. If each new round of fighting adds to the cost without producing a decisive political result, the United States will find itself spending more while moving no closer to its goals.
The Strait of Hormuz gives Iran a way to increase this pressure. Disruption to shipping can keep energy markets unstable and raise the economic cost of the conflict well beyond the battlefield. The longer the disruption continues, the more difficult it becomes for Washington to separate its military campaign from its effects on the American economy.
The question is whether the United States can continue to bear the full cost of the conflict if the economic pressure grows while the chance of achieving its objectives declines. At some stage, American administration may conclude that continuing the war will bring more damage than benefit. That would create the conditions for an American retreat. If Washington withdraws without achieving its main goals, the result could be a strategic defeat, even if American forces remain far stronger than Iran’s in conventional military terms.
Why China could benefit
Such an outcome would also affect the wider balance of power. China is already benefiting from a war that consumes American resources, damages Washington’s reputation and reduces its ability to focus on other strategic priorities. Beijing does not need to defeat the United States directly. It can benefit simply by watching Americas useless overstretch. The war also gives China an opportunity to question whether the United States can keep its commitments to allies in Asia. China would also suffer from high energy prices and disruptions to trade. But if the United States emerges from the war with fewer resources, greater economic pressure and damaged credibility, China could gain room to expand its influence without taking on the costs of a direct military confrontation.
This is one reason the outcome of the war matters beyond the Middle East. A costly American withdrawal could affect how allies and rivals judge US power. Countries that depend on Washington for security may question its ability to sustain a long conflict. Rivals may become more willing to challenge American influence in other regions.
Could this be America’s Suez?
The Suez Crisis did not single-handedly end British power. Britain’s relative decline had been developing for decades, and the United States had already become the leading Western power. But Suez made the change unmistakable. Britain had launched a heavy military operation and then had to withdraw under financial and political pressure. But the crisis clearly exposed the limits of its ability to act as a global power.
A similar outcome is possible for the United States in Iran. If the war becomes more costly with time, if energy prices continue to place pressure on American households and businesses, and if Washington cannot achieve its main objectives, the economic logic for continuing the conflict may become increasingly weak. A withdrawal without a clear political achievement would then damage the credibility of American power as a world superpower.
The United States is not Britain in 1956. Its international position will not collapse because of one war. Yet these advantages do not remove the basic problem: US may ruin its credit as super power of current international order.
The real test will come when Washington has to choose between continuing an expensive war and accepting a retreat. If it leaves Iran without achieving its goals, the consequences could extend far beyond the battlefield. The war could become a turning point that speeds up the decline of American order and gives other powers more room to shape the coming international order. Such scenario would be what could make Hormuz America’s Suez.

articles.title: The great divorce: Why Russia must turn away from Europe
articles.body:
The great divorce: Why Russia must turn away from Europe
In Russia, many people, driven by lingering Europhilia and habits formed during the second half of the 20th century, when Western Europe enjoyed a period of relative peace following its defeat, continue to look for signs of its ‘recovery’ and ways to restore relations.
There are forces within Russia that would advocate overcoming the current hostility and there are decent people in Western Europe, too, even if they are increasingly marginalized. But the causes of this outbreak of desperate Russophobia run deep and cannot easily be remedied and overcoming them may require the complete defeat and dismantling of much of the current European elite. But achieving that goal could come at too high a cost.
I shall attempt to analyze the causes of the almost unprecedented hostility towards Russia among the elites of most European countries and offer recommendations for Russian policy towards Western Europe.
I have written more than once that Peter the Great’s journey towards the rest of Europe, which initially brought many benefits, including helping to create some of the world’s greatest literature and music and modernizing the armed forces, continued for a century and a half longer than was necessary or beneficial.
For many centuries, Europe was the principal source of evil in the world, offering endless wars, including two world wars within a single generation, repeated genocides, colonialism, racism and other calamities.
For Russians who grew up in the shadow of Peter the Great and Catherine the Great, and who internalized a love of Europe, it’s not easy to acknowledge this simple truth and act accordingly.
Russian Europhilia was greatly reinforced when Western Europe, having been overwhelmed by the torrent of evil it had unleashed, became relatively peaceful for a time during the second half of the 20th century. In the USSR, Europhilia was fueled by the everyday hardships of Soviet socialism, contrasted with the far greater material prosperity of the western part of the half-continent.
There are many reasons for the current anti-Russian hysteria. The main one is the all-encompassing, multi-layered crisis that has gripped the western part of Europe and this crisis is particularly painful after decades of relative prosperity and, above all, the euphoria of victory that swept the West following the collapse of the USSR.
That euphoria temporarily obscured the mounting signs of crisis in European economies and societies, which had already become apparent by the end of the 1960s, when a mood of protest was beginning to take hold. And then a miracle happened as the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc provided hundreds of millions of eager new consumers and millions of cheap workers.
From the 2000s onwards, these problems resurfaced with renewed force. A decade later, most Western European countries had fallen into stagnation as inequality began to worsen once again. Living standards for much of the population began to decline, while competitors started pulling ahead, not only the US and China, but also many countries of the Global South.
Euphoria gave way to a sense of failure and European elites are now trying to drown out that feeling by fueling hostility towards Russia.
At the same time, from the end of the 20th century, the consequences of the anti-colonial revolutions of the 1950s and 1960s began to make themselves felt. The flow of resources that Europe had extracted from the rest of the world since the 16th century, and upon which its prosperity and cultural, military, scientific and technological leadership had largely been built, began to dry up.
An unusually long period of relative peace and prosperity brought to the surface some of the worst traits of the European character and heritage as Western Europe began to turn its back on humanism and the desire to serve the common good.
Decades of development in a climate of peace and formal democracy have led to the degradation of the ruling elites because democratic political systems are anti-meritocratic. The majority elect those who resemble themselves, or even those who are worse, and in the best cases, they elect shrewd manipulators.
One of the most significant causes of Western Europe’s current decline, and to a lesser extent, that of other parts of the collective West, is the rejection of faith.
This began with the Age of Enlightenment, which created the conditions for the decline of people who, consciously or unconsciously, set about rejecting the divine, the best within themselves.
I finally realized that Western Europe had taken a sharp and irreversible downward turn in the early 2000s, when following lengthy debates over the European Union’s proposed constitution, it was decided not to mention Christianity as its spiritual foundation.
Losing its footing and falling behind in economic and spiritual competition, Western Europe is reverting to one of the worst traits of its civilization, which is militarism.
The militarization of the economy is seen as one of the principal ways out of economic decline and militarization requires an enemy. As so often before, that enemy has been identified as Russia as the image of the enemy is being inflated practically out of thin air.
We must tell ourselves firmly, we are not Europeans, but an independent northern Eurasian civilization whose external spiritual roots lie in the south and east.
Our traditional religions came to us from the south, from Byzantium, Palestine, and the Arab and Buddhist worlds. Our political culture stems from the east, from two and a half centuries of interaction and conflict with the Great Mongol Empire, of which the territory of modern-day China was historically a part.
The Mongols plundered, but they didn’t suppress religion, language or culture and we would never have become Great Russia, the world’s largest and one of its most culturally, nationally and religiously open countries, united through a rigid vertical hierarchy of power centered on the Russian people and the Russian language, had it not been for the Mongol political and ideological legacy.
From Western Europe, which, relying on its military superiority, took the lead in education during the 17th and 18th centuries, we sought to adopt the European Bologna system.
Yet that system is increasingly anti-meritocratic as it churns out poorly educated people on a mass scale, many of whom are now coming to power. Let me remind you that some of the earliest institutions of higher learning were established in North Africa and Byzantium.
Some of our more affluent fellow citizens still send their children to study in Europe, ‘abroad’, where as I have seen time and again, they often lose more skills and talents than they acquire.
Our military doctrine contains a clear directive and in circumstances of extreme necessity, provides for the possibility of nuclear strikes against key European countries that are fueling anti-Russian hysteria while simultaneously supporting the war in Ukraine.
Our restraint and peacefulness over recent decades have proved counterproductive. They have contributed to the resurgence of the worst aspects of European political culture so Western Europe must therefore face firm deterrence.
But at the same time, we must remember that we are a country of Pushkin, Tchaikovsky, Dostoevsky, and Tvardovsky, as well as Goethe, Dante, Shakespeare, Mozart and countless others.
Culturally, we must not cut ourselves off from Europe. Rather, we must develop and nurture our Asian roots, of which we have foolishly been ashamed.
The main direction of our internal spiritual, economic and political development must be a shift towards Siberia as there, in the east and north, lies Russia’s future.
We must finally acknowledge that we are not an Eastern European civilization, but a northern Eurasian one, among the most open to the world.
We must also recognize, however difficult it may be, that ‘European-ness’, in the present circumstances, is increasingly becoming a sign of intellectual narrow-mindedness and moral duplicity.
And given the current orientation of European elites, it is simply harmful to us, the representatives of the great multinational, multi-confessional and multicultural Russian people.
Our country-civilization must at last become, for all of us, Russian Yakuts, Russian Buryats, Russian Ossetians, Russian Tatars, Russian Belarusians, Russian Great Russians and others, an independent northern Eurasian civilization.
Europe, in its present and foreseeable future condition, must end at our borders.
This however, is not a call for a new Iron Curtain, but for a rational, modern policy directed towards the future.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by RT.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones reportedly strike major shopping mall in Russia’s Belgorod overnight
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces reportedly struck the MegaGRINN shopping and entertainment complex in the Russian city of Belgorod during a mass drone attack overnight on 25 October, when the mall was closed and no visitors were inside, according to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.
Russian authorities reported that a civilian was killed and 10 people were injured in the broader mass drone attack on Belgorod. One of the injured was an ambulance worker, according to the regional operational headquarters.
The majority of the drones reportedly targeted one area in the city center, according to ASTRA.
Belgorod’s largest shopping complex targeted
Exilenova+ identified the reported target as MegaGRINN, Belgorod’s largest shopping and entertainment complex covering about 163,000 square meters. The facility houses more than 200 stores, a supermarket, restaurants, a cinema, and entertainment areas.
Belgorod is a Russian city about 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Ukraine’s northeastern border and roughly 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Kharkiv. The city and surrounding oblast have repeatedly come under Ukrainian drone attacks during Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.
Belgorod Oblast borders Ukraine’s Sumy, Kharkiv, and Luhansk oblasts. Russian forces have used the region to launch missile and drone attacks on Ukraine and to stage ground offensives across the border.
Update: Ukraine’s General Staff reports strikes on Russian radar stations in Belgorod Oblast
Update 18:00: Ukraine’s General Staff said Ukrainian forces struck Russian radar stations near Hostishchevo and Kurgannoye in Russia’s Belgorod Oblast on 24 October and overnight on 25 October.
The General Staff said the strikes would create gaps in Russian radar coverage and expand Ukraine’s ability to use unmanned systems.
The update did not mention an attack on Belgorod city or the shopping mall.
Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian retail infrastructure
The reported strike comes amid an intensified Russian campaign against Ukrainian retail and logistics infrastructure. These attacks have included strikes on shopping centers during business hours, including a 21 August Russian drone attack on the crowded Soniachna Halereia mall in Kryvyi Rih, where 16 people were killed and more than 120 injured.
The reported strike on MegaGRINN took place overnight, when the complex was reportedly closed and empty of visitors. Russian authorities reported casualties from the wider attack on Belgorod, but have not linked them to the mall.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says it downed 2 missiles fired by Houthis
articles.body:
(Reuters) -- Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war, Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden.
Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements, though they reported missile debris falling near the site of one of the purported oil targets. It was not immediately clear if any of the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif.
Saudi Civil Defense said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Mecca and Medina regions, home to Islam's holiest sites visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims every year.
It said parts of the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while debris also fell in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. It was not clear if that was linked to the Houthis' reported targeting of the Rabigh oil refinery.
Shortly after that, Houthis denied that they attacked Mecca and Medina, saying that their operations "target Saudi oil facilities and military bases."
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognized government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilization there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

articles.title: Bulgaria votes for president in election dominated by Ukraine war and the economy
articles.body:
The campaign has focused on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and an increase in drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria's coast in the Black Sea, as well as rising energy prices and inflation.
Bulgarians are heading to the polls to elect their president on Sunday, in a campaign that has mostly revolved around growing concerns over the economy and drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea.
The vote will be the first major test of Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party since it came out on top in parliamentary elections last April.
Despite a record 27 candidates, the race is expected to be decided in a runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who is backed by Radev's party and favours dialogue with Moscow while opposing military aid to Ukraine, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is backed by pro-Western opposition parties.
Yotova is expected to win between 41% and 47% of the vote, while Gyurov is polling between 28% and 31%.
The leader of the pro-Russian far-right Vazrazhdane party, Kostadin Kostadinov, is in third place on 10-13%.
The campaign has focused heavily on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria’s coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and NATO member country.
The strikes have raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict, while also compelling the government to ask Bulgaria's partners for assistance to strengthen its maritime security.
Candidates have also looked to respond to public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet.
Two main candidates among record total of 27
Main frontrunner Yotova took over this year as president of Bulgaria when Rumen Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections, eventually becoming prime minister.
If successful she would become the first woman ever elected president in Bulgaria's history. A win for Yotova would be a boost for Radev, who has also called for dialogue with Moscow.
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Yotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
Her main challenger is economist Andrey Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister in the first few months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition.
Gyurov has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, and signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership.
Polling stations will close at 8 pm local time, after which initial exit polls will be announced while preliminary results are expected on Monday.
Turnout must be above 50%, and the winner needs a majority of votes. Projections have Sunday’s turnout at less than 40%, indicating a likely runoff on 1 November.

articles.title: US updates travel warnings for 13 Middle Eastern countries
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US updates travel warnings for 13 Middle Eastern countries
The United States has updated travel advisories for 13 countries across the Middle East, citing the risk of further attacks by Yemen’s Houthis and alleged Iranian efforts to target American officials in the region. The revisions come alongside reductions in staffing at several US embassies amid concerns over a wider escalation.
The advisories, dated 23 October, cover Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen. The updates revise the security warnings rather than raise the countries’ existing advisory levels.
"The possibility of regional effects, including the potential for flight disruptions, makes a region-wide advisory update important and prudent," a State Department official said in comments shared by PBS correspondent Nick Schifrin.
The department said the revisions reflected increased potential for armed attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US government officials. Those claims come amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition, including missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory.
Advisories by country, and what they mean:
Eight countries are listed at Level 3, meaning Americans should reconsider travel, while five remain at Level 4 — "do not travel", the State Department’s highest warning. The country-specific warnings are:
- Bahrain: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Iran: Level 4 — Do not travel. Washington cites unrest, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism, wrongful detention and other risks.
- Iraq: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- Israel: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and unrest.
- Jordan: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Kuwait: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. Washington cites crime and other risks.
- Lebanon: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- Oman: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Qatar: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists “other” risks, rather than a separate terrorism, crime or unrest indicator.
- Saudi Arabia: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks. The update follows Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, including the 10 October strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
- Syria: Level 4 — Do not travel. Washington cites unrest, crime, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
- United Arab Emirates: Level 3 — Reconsider travel. The advisory lists terrorism and other security risks.
- Yemen: Level 4 — Do not travel. The advisory lists unrest, crime, health risks, kidnapping or hostage-taking, terrorism and other risks.
US authorities have urged Americans to monitor embassy alerts and airline operations, prepare for possible flight cancellations or airspace closures, and maintain emergency departure plans that do not depend on US government assistance. They also recommend enrolling in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program to receive security updates.
The warnings follow Friday’s reports that Washington was reducing staffing at its embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE. Axios first reported an intelligence memo alleging that Iranian plots against American personnel had reached "advanced stages"; the Associated Press subsequently obtained the memo and confirmed the staffing reductions with US officials.
Those four embassies remain open under restricted operations, and personnel are not subject to the same compulsory departure order issued on Wednesday for non-essential US staff and their families in Saudi Arabia.
US officials have denied that the staffing changes are linked to prospective new US or Israeli strikes on Iran. The advisory updates themselves do not establish that another military operation is imminent, although the move comes amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, with US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warning that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran before the upcoming US midterm elections.

articles.title: FP-1 drones traveled more than 2,500 km and struck two facilities in Omsk: the "Omsk Rubber" plant and an OZON warehouse were hit
articles.body:
FP-1 drones traveled more than 2,500 km and struck two facilities in Omsk: the "Omsk Rubber" plant and an OZON warehouse were hit
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian FP-1 drones traveled more than 2,500 km and struck the "Omsk Rubber" plant and an OZON warehouse in Omsk. The plant accounts for about 25% of rubber production in the Russian Federation.
Ukrainian long-range FP-1 drones struck two sites at once in Russia’s Omsk on the evening of October 24, covering more than 2,500 km from the border. The targets were Omsk Rubber, one of the largest petrochemical plants in the Russian Federation, and the logistics warehouse complex of the OZON marketplace. UNN reports this, citing the company’s Telegram channel, Fire Point, the drone manufacturer.
Details
The FP-1 drones covered more than 2,500 km from the border and struck two sites at once in Omsk
Fire Point said that the Defense Forces attacked the Omsk Rubber plant, one of the largest petrochemical enterprises in the Russian Federation. According to previously published data, the enterprise accounted for about 25% of Russia’s production of butadiene-styrene rubbers.
The logistics warehouse complex of OZON was also traditionally targeted
Denys Shtilerman, co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, also reposted the moment of the strike in Omsk, which was published on "X".
Additionally
The night before, on October 24, FP-1 drones struck another enterprise in the Russian Federation’s rubber industry - the Tolyattikauchuk plant in the Samara region, which, according to Fire Point, accounts for about 25% of the Russian synthetic rubber market. The plant’s products are used in the production of Russian weapons, including ballistic missiles.
Omsk, located more than 2,500 km from the border, has not been targeted by FP-1 drones for the first time: previously, they attacked the Omsk Oil Refinery, the largest oil refinery in the Russian Federation, several times, most recently on October 8.
